ui.empty: No kindergarten-to-grade-5 solution on Saving Planets is pinned to this region yet.

americas.sum: 4ocean removes plastic from oceans, rivers, and coastlines with full-time cleanup crews, funded by products made from recovered plastic.
eli: What is it? Full-time professional captains and cleanup crews recover plastic and trash from oceans, rivers, and coastlines every day. The model: each bracelet or product sold funds the removal of one pound of trash, and recovered material is sorted, shredded, and turned into recycled products.

Why does it matter? Plastic harms marine wildlife, breaks into microplastics , and persists for decades. 4ocean's founders saw beaches buried in garbage on a surf trip to Bali in 2015 and built a business that pays crews to remove it every day.
americas.alt: 4ocean: Full-Time Crews Removing Ocean Plastic
americas.credit: Created by SI and Biological SI Partner

americas.sum: Each year, Adopt-a-Beach volunteers remove tens of thousands of pounds of litter from Great Lakes beaches, about 85% of it plastic.
eli: Adopt-a-Beach is when people go to a beach on the Great Lakes and pick up trash.
Most of the trash they find is plastic.
They also write down what they find, so scientists can learn where the trash comes from.

src.name: Alliance for the Great Lakes, Adopt-a-Beach

americas.alt: Adopt-a-Beach (Alliance for the Great Lakes)

americas.sum: More than 20 kelp farms grow ribbon, giant, bull and sugar kelp in Alaska's cold, nutrient-rich waters (Alaska Mariculture Alliance).
eli: Kelp is a big seaweed that grows fast in cold ocean water.
Alaska farmers grow it on lines in the sea and harvest it each spring and early summer.
It becomes food, farm and beauty products, and it takes up carbon and extra nutrients from the water.

src.name: McKinley Research Group for the Alaska Mariculture Cluster, Alaska Mariculture Industry Update, Spring 2026

americas.alt: Alaska Kelp and Seaweed Farming
places: Kodiak, Alaska (Alaska Sea Grant mariculture specialists)
Kasaan Bay, Southeast Alaska (new kelp farm leases)

americas.n: Alaska SeaLife Center: Marine Wildlife Rescue
americas.sum: The Alaska SeaLife Center in Seward is a nonprofit aquarium and research center that rescues stranded marine animals and studies Alaska's marine ecosystems.
eli: Sometimes baby seals and sea otters lose their mothers or get hurt.
The Alaska SeaLife Center brings them to Seward and cares for them day and night.
Its scientists also study sea lions and seabirds to learn how the ocean is changing.
americas.alt: Alaska SeaLife Center: Marine Wildlife Rescue

americas.sum: Since 1875, American Forests has worked to restore U.S. forests, from big natural landscapes to city streets, with more than 63 million trees planted.
eli: American Forests is one of the oldest forest groups in the United States.
It plants trees in big forests and in city neighborhoods that need shade.
Trees clean the air, cool hot streets and give animals homes.
americas.alt: Ponderosa pine seedlings being planted to restore a burned area of Dixie National Forest in Utah
americas.credit: Image: Intermountain Region US Forest Service (public domain)

americas.sum: American Rivers has worked directly on more than 200 dam removals; in 2025 the U.S. removed 100 dams and reconnected more than 4,893 river miles.
eli: American Rivers is a group that helps take out old dams that are not needed anymore.
When a dam comes out, fish can swim up the river again.
In 2025, 100 dams came out in the U.S., freeing almost 5,000 miles of river.
americas.alt: American Rivers
americas.credit: Created by SI and Biological SI Partner

americas.sum: Since 1972, the Arbor Day Foundation says it has planted more than half a billion trees, working in more than 60 countries (nonprofit figures).
eli: The Arbor Day Foundation is a group that plants trees.
It has helped plant more than 500 million trees.
Trees clean the air, give animals homes and help cool the planet.
americas.alt: Volunteers carrying young red spruce trees to planting sites on Pisgah National Forest in North Carolina
americas.credit: Image: Gary Peeples/USFWS (public domain)

americas.sum: Close to 4,000 robotic floats dive through the ocean and send back temperature and salinity data, free to everyone. The 3 millionth profile came in 2024.
eli: Argo floats are robots that sink deep into the ocean and come back up.
On the way they measure how warm and how salty the water is.
They send the numbers to a satellite, and anyone can use them for free.
americas.alt: A Deep SOLO ocean float being lowered into the sea from a research ship
places: Argo Program Office, Scripps Institution of Oceanography, San Diego

americas.sum: A satellite system that tracks wildlife and ocean instruments from tiny transmitters, following more than 8,000 animals every month for conservation science.
eli: Scientists put a tiny radio tag on a turtle, bird or whale.
Satellites pick up the tag's signal and work out where the animal is.
Knowing where animals travel helps people protect them.

src.name: NOAA OSPO, Argos Data Collection System

americas.alt: An adult false killer whale surfacing off Guam, photographed by NOAA scientists before a satellite tag was attached
americas.credit: Image: Adam U / NOAA/NMFS/Pacific Islands Fisheries Science Center (public domain)
places: NOAA Office of Satellite and Product Operations, Suitland, Maryland

americas.n: ATLAS Asteroid Terrestrial-impact Last Alert System
americas.sum: Four robotic telescopes, two in Hawaiʻi, search the entire dark sky every 24 hours for asteroids that could hit Earth, so people can be warned.
eli: ATLAS is four robot telescopes that scan the night sky.
They look for space rocks that come close to Earth.
An early warning gives people time to get ready or move away.

src.name: NASA, ATLAS now capable of full-sky search

americas.alt: The island of Hawaiʻi, home of Mauna Loa, seen from the International Space Station
places: ATLAS telescope, Mauna Loa, Hawaiʻi Island
ATLAS telescope, El Sauce Observatory, Chile

americas.sum: In Oregon's Bridge Creek, beavers given simple dam starters raised juvenile steelhead survival 52% and production 175% (NOAA Fisheries).
eli: What is it? Beaver dam analogs: simple structures beavers build on, raising water and reconnecting streams to floodplains.
Why does it matter? Eroded, trenched streams had stranded plants and harmed steelhead; beaver dams bring water back.

How does it help people? Steelhead were once abundant across the Northwest before beavers were trapped out; restored streams that produce nearly twice as many young fish support the fisheries people rely on.

src.name: NOAA Fisheries, Oregon beavers engineer better fish habitat

americas.alt: A beaver dam holding back a large wetland in St. Louis County, Minnesota, with a beaver lodge in the distance
americas.credit: Image: Courtney Celley/USFWS (public domain)

americas.sum: A New York nonprofit restoring the harbor with oyster reefs, aiming for one billion oysters by 2030 (nonprofit figures).
eli: What is it? Oyster reef restoration, shell recycling and harbor education.
Why does it matter? Reefs are habitat, and restoring them engages a whole city in its harbor.
americas.alt: Billion Oyster Project – Oceans

americas.sum: In January 2023, the U.S. EPA used Clean Water Act section 404(c) to limit mine waste disposal in Bristol Bay headwaters near the Pebble deposit.
eli: Bristol Bay in Alaska has rivers full of wild salmon.
A large copper and gold mine was proposed near streams where many of those salmon start life.
The U.S. government limited where mine waste could go, and a judge is now deciding whether that decision stands.

src.name: Alaska Department of Fish and Game, 2025 Bristol Bay Area Annual Management Report (May 2026)

americas.alt: Bristol Bay Salmon Habitat Protection (EPA)
americas.credit: Image: NASA Earth Observatory image by Joshua Stevens, using MODIS data from LANCE/EOSDIS Rapid Response
places: Pebble deposit area, Bristol Bay watershed, Alaska

americas.sum: A NASA-funded survey in Arizona that has discovered more near-Earth objects than any other: 17,930 near-Earth asteroids since 1995.
eli: Catalina is a team in Arizona that hunts for space rocks every clear night.
They have found more near-Earth asteroids than anyone else.
They even spotted a small one hours before it burned up over Africa.
americas.alt: Discovery images of asteroid 2018 LA, a faint moving dot, taken hours before it entered Earth's atmosphere
places: Lunar and Planetary Laboratory, University of Arizona, Tucson

americas.sum: Since 1966, the Chesapeake Bay Foundation has worked to save the Bay and its rivers, adding more than 21 million oysters in fiscal year 2026 (CBF).
eli: The Chesapeake Bay is a huge bay fed by many rivers.
Oysters clean the water, so this group grows and plants millions of them.
They also plant trees by streams and teach students outdoors.
americas.alt: Chesapeake Bay Foundation – Rivers

americas.sum: Clean Lakes Alliance works to improve water quality in Madison's Yahara lakes; it reports 81 monitoring stations and over $1.4 million in grants (its figures).
eli: Madison, Wisconsin, has five lakes connected by the Yahara River.
Too much phosphorus washes in and feeds smelly algae blooms.
Volunteers check the lakes and the group helps pay for projects to keep them clean.

americas.sum: Clean Up the Lake removes submerged litter from freshwater lakes using scuba divers and volunteers, and GPS-pins, sorts and weighs every piece it finds.
eli: What is it? Underwater and shoreline cleanups of freshwater lakes, with every piece of litter GPS-pinned, categorized, and weighed. They also run aquatic invasive species monitoring and youth education programs.
Why does it matter? Most lake litter sinks out of sight, where it leaches fuel, oil, and heavy metals for decades. Removing it protects water quality, wildlife, and the recreation millions depend on.

src.name: Clean Up The Lake, Litter Stats

americas.alt: Lake Tahoe, Pyramid Lake and the snow-capped Sierra Nevada seen from the International Space Station

americas.n: Cool Earth Basic Income Pilot (Peruvian Amazon)
americas.sum: Cool Earth gave 211 Indigenous people in three communities in Peru's central Amazon an unconditional basic income for two years (University of Bath).
eli: Some families in the Amazon rainforest have very little money.
A charity gave each person a small amount of money every few months, to spend however they wanted.
Families ate better, stayed home instead of leaving for work, and planted and protected more forest.

src.name: University of Bath, World-first basic income trial boosts Indigenous livelihoods and Amazon rainforest protection (20 Oct. 2026)

americas.alt: Cool Earth Basic Income Pilot (Peruvian Amazon)
americas.credit: Image: Heiner Amado Cadillo via Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 3.0)
places: Central Peruvian Amazon, Peru (approximate area of the pilot communities)

americas.sum: NOAA's Coral Reef Watch uses satellites to warn of the ocean heat that bleaches corals, with daily monitoring of 95% of the world's coral reefs.
eli: Corals are tiny animals that build reefs, and too much heat makes them turn white.
NOAA satellites check the ocean's temperature every day.
Reef managers use the warnings to protect corals before it is too late.

src.name: NOAA Coral Reef Watch, Satellite Bleaching Alert emails

americas.alt: Reefs of the Great Barrier Reef off the coast of Queensland, Australia, seen from the International Space Station
places: NOAA Center for Weather and Climate Prediction, College Park, Maryland

americas.sum: Coral Restoration Foundation had returned 253,833 corals to Florida's reefs by the end of 2024 (organization figure). Florida's Coral Reef in the Florida Keys.
eli: What is it? Offshore coral nurseries and large-scale outplanting of nursery-grown corals.
Why does it matter? Replanting nursery-grown corals helps damaged reefs recover faster than they could alone.
americas.alt: Coral Restoration Foundation – Oceans
americas.credit: Image: NASA/GSFC/METI/ERSDAC/JAROS and U.S./Japan ASTER Science Team (PIA03890)

americas.sum: Coral Vita grows reef-building corals on land up to 50 times faster than in nature, and says it has grown over 100,000 corals (company figures).
eli: Coral reefs are dying in many places around the world.
Coral Vita grows baby corals in tanks on land, where they grow very fast.
Then divers plant them back on damaged reefs.
americas.alt: Adopt a Coral
places: Grand Bahama, The Bahamas (Coral Vita coral farm)

americas.n: Costa Rica Payments for Environmental Services (FONAFIFO)
americas.sum: Costa Rica's FONAFIFO pays the owners of forests and forest plantations for the environmental services they provide, under Forestry Law 7575 (FONAFIFO).
eli: Forests clean the air, keep water safe and give animals a home.
In Costa Rica the government pays forest owners for those services.
So keeping trees standing becomes worth it for the people who own the land.
americas.alt: Costa Rica Payments for Environmental Services (FONAFIFO)

americas.sum: NASA's EPIC camera rides on NOAA's DSCOVR spacecraft at the L1 point, photographing the entire sunlit face of Earth several times a day, with an archive...
eli: What is it? A camera photographing the entire sunlit face of Earth several times a day.
Why does it matter? Daily whole-Earth views, including ozone measurements, track our changing planet.
americas.alt: DSCOVR / EPIC (NASA–NOAA)
places: NOAA Satellite Operations Facility, Suitland, Maryland (mission control)

americas.sum: Two Elwha River dams came down between 2011 and 2014, and more than 20 million tons of trapped sediment flowed downstream to rebuild the river and coast.
eli: The Elwha River had two dams that stopped salmon from swimming home.
Between 2011 and 2014 both dams were taken down.
Sand and gravel stuck behind the dams washed down the river and helped rebuild the beach, and the river runs free again.

src.name: National Park Service, Elwha River Restoration

americas.alt: Olympic National Park on Washington's Olympic Peninsula, home of the Elwha River, seen by Landsat 8

americas.sum: NASA's EMIT instrument on the International Space Station maps the minerals in desert dust and has spotted methane super-emitters from space (NASA JPL).
eli: EMIT is a special camera on the International Space Station.
It splits sunlight into many colors to tell what the ground is made of.
It also spotted big leaks of methane , a gas that heats the planet, so they can be fixed.
americas.alt: EMIT (NASA) – Earth Observation

americas.sum: Earth Fire Alliance's FireSat satellites are built to spot wildfires as small as 5 by 5 meters from space and get the data to firefighters fast.
eli: Wildfires are much easier to stop while they are still small.
FireSat satellites carry special cameras that can sense heat from space.
They can spot a fire about the size of two parking spaces and help firefighters act fast.

src.name: Earth Fire Alliance, FireSat first light (Sep 16, 2026)

americas.alt: FireSat (Earth Fire Alliance)

americas.sum: ESA's FORUM will measure Earth's outgoing far-infrared radiation, never measured from space before, filling a missing piece of the climate jigsaw (ESA).
eli: Earth gives off heat into space as invisible infrared light.
Part of that light, called far-infrared, has never been measured from space.
FORUM will measure it, helping scientists understand how Earth keeps its heat balance.
americas.alt: NOAA world map of the infrared (longwave) energy Earth sends back out to space
americas.credit: Image: NOAA NESDIS (public domain)
places: Europe's Spaceport, Kourou, French Guiana (planned launch site)

americas.sum: Galápagos Conservancy and the Galápagos National Park Directorate rear giant tortoises in breeding centres and return them to their home islands.
eli: Giant tortoises once covered the Galápagos Islands, but people and animals they brought nearly wiped them out.
Park rangers and scientists raise baby tortoises in safe centres until they are big enough to survive.
Then they carry them back to the islands where they belong.
americas.alt: Galápagos Giant Tortoise Rewilding

americas.sum: GEDI fires lasers from the International Space Station to measure the height and 3D shape of Earth's forests (University of Maryland).
eli: GEDI is a laser tool on the International Space Station.
It shines light down on forests and times how long it takes to bounce back.
That tells scientists how tall trees are and how much carbon forests hold.

src.name: University of Maryland, GEDI mission overview

americas.alt: The GEDI forest-mapping laser instrument mounted outside Japan's Kibo module on the International Space Station
places: University of Maryland, College Park (mission lead)

americas.sum: NOAA's next generation of geostationary weather satellites, planned from 2032, will improve warnings of severe weather and hazards (NOAA).
eli: GeoXO will be new weather satellites that stay over the same spot above Earth.
They will watch storms, wildfires, smoke and floods as they happen.
This helps forecasters warn people sooner.
americas.alt: Visualization of the planned GeoXO East satellite above Earth with the scanning pattern of its ocean color instrument
americas.credit: Image: NASA's Scientific Visualization Studio (public domain)

americas.sum: Global Fishing Watch uses satellites and SI to map fishing; its 2024 Nature study found about 75% of industrial fishing vessels are not publicly tracked.
eli: Big fishing ships sail all over the ocean, and many of them are hard to see.
Global Fishing Watch uses pictures from space and smart computers to find them.
They put the map online for free, so everyone can see where fishing happens and protect the ocean.
americas.alt: A small dory with a high prow setting out from a commercial fishing vessel at sea
americas.credit: Image: Alaska Fisheries Science Center, Marine Observer Program (public domain)

americas.sum: Free satellite forest data and deforestation alerts from WRI; where Indigenous forest monitors used it, deforestation fell 52% in one year.
eli: Global Forest Watch is a free map of the world's forests made from satellite pictures.
When trees are cut down, the map sends an alert.
People who live in forests use the alerts to stop illegal cutting fast.

src.name: Global Forest Watch (now Global Nature Watch), Our History

americas.alt: Global Forest Watch (WRI) – Forests

americas.sum: Globe at Night invites anyone to measure how dark their night sky is. People have sent 331,147 observations to track light pollution (program figures).
eli: At night, city lights can hide the stars.
Globe at Night asks people to go outside, find a group of stars and say how many they can see.
All those answers show where the sky is too bright, so we can fix it.
americas.alt: Globe at Night (NSF NOIRLab) – Space

americas.sum: Twin US-German satellites weigh Earth's water by measuring gravity, tracking groundwater, ice and sea level since 2018. Active.
eli: What is it? Twin satellites measuring Earth's changing gravity field.
Why does it matter? To track water in aquifers, ice and oceans, for drought and water planning.
americas.alt: GRACE-FO (NASA / Germany)

americas.sum: The Great Lakes Plastic Cleanup captures plastic across the world's largest freshwater system using Seabins, drones, and beach robots.
eli: What is it? Deploying proven capture technology — Seabins, PixieDrones, BeBots, and stormwater LittaTraps — to remove plastic from marinas, shorelines, and drains before it reaches open water, plus community science to characterize what is found.

Why does it matter? An estimated 10 million kilograms of plastic litter enter the Great Lakes each year. Capturing it at the source protects drinking water, wildlife, and the 107 million people who live in the region.

src.name: Great Lakes Plastic Cleanup, 2025 season data (May 26, 2026)

americas.alt: Great Lakes Plastic Cleanup

americas.n: Gulf of Alaska Keeper: Marine Debris Cleanup
americas.sum: Gulf of Alaska Keeper (GoAK) is a nonprofit that removes marine debris from the remote shores of Prince William Sound and the northern Gulf of Alaska (GoAK).
eli: Ocean currents carry nets, ropes and plastic to faraway Alaska beaches where nobody lives.
Gulf of Alaska Keeper crews and volunteers pick it up and pack it into giant bags.
Helicopters lift the bags to a barge, and the trash goes to Anchorage to be recycled or thrown away safely.
americas.alt: Gulf of Alaska Keeper: Marine Debris Cleanup
places: Montague Island, Prince William Sound, Alaska

americas.sum: Since 1985, Heal the Bay has worked to make the coastal waters and watersheds of Greater Los Angeles safe, healthy and clean (Heal the Bay).
eli: Heal the Bay helps keep the beaches and ocean near Los Angeles clean.
Thousands of volunteers pick up trash on special cleanup days.
They also run a small aquarium where kids meet local sea animals.

americas.sum: Since 1986, more than 19 million volunteers have collected more than 400 million pounds of trash from beaches and waterways (Ocean Conservancy).
eli: Every year, people around the world clean trash off beaches and rivers on the same day.
They also write down what they find.
That list helps find ways to stop trash from reaching the ocean.
americas.alt: Two volunteers picking up trash on Second Beach in Olympic Coast National Marine Sanctuary during the International Coastal Cleanup
americas.credit: Image: Karlyn Langjahr/NOAA (public domain)
places: Texas coast, where the first Cleanup was held in 1986

americas.n: Keep Tahoe Blue (League to Save Lake Tahoe)
americas.sum: Keep Tahoe Blue, the League to Save Lake Tahoe, has protected the lake for decades, and its volunteers picked up 1,330 pounds of litter after July 4, 2026.
eli: Lake Tahoe is famous for its clear blue water.
After the Fourth of July, volunteers clean up beaches so trash doesn't reach the lake.
Keep Tahoe Blue uses science to keep the lake clear for people and fish.

src.name: Keep Tahoe Blue, Early history of the League

americas.alt: Keep Tahoe Blue (League to Save Lake Tahoe)

americas.sum: Once straightened into a canal, Florida's Kissimmee River is winding again: 44 miles of river and 20,000 acres of wetlands restored (SFWMD).
eli: Long ago, people dug a straight canal through the curvy Kissimmee River.
That stopped floods but hurt the wetlands, birds and fish.
Now workers have filled parts of the canal so the river can curve and flood its wetlands again.

src.name: South Florida Water Management District, Kissimmee River

americas.alt: Aerial view of the restored, winding Kissimmee River beside a backfilled canal
americas.credit: Image: U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (public domain)

americas.sum: Four Klamath River dams came out by October 2024, reopening more than 400 miles of habitat to salmon, steelhead and lamprey (Klamath River Renewal).
eli: Dams are walls across rivers. On the Klamath River, four big dams stopped salmon from swimming upstream for about 100 years.
In 2024 all four dams were taken out.
Now salmon can swim to more than 400 miles of river again, and people are planting new plants where the old lakes were.

src.name: NOAA Fisheries, Final step in Klamath River dam removal

americas.alt: Klamath River Dam Removal – Rivers
americas.credit: Image: NASA/METI/AIST/Japan Space Systems and U.S./Japan ASTER Science Team (PIA26448)

americas.n: Lake Erie Harmful Algal Bloom Forecast (NOAA)
americas.sum: NOAA forecasts and tracks toxic algae in western Lake Erie through the summer so cities and swimmers can keep drinking water and people safe (NOAA NCCOS).
eli: Sometimes tiny green living things called algae grow so much in Lake Erie that the water turns green.
Some of this algae makes poison that can get into drinking water.
NOAA watches the lake from space and from boats and warns people where the bad water is, like a weather report.

src.name: NOAA NCCOS, Western Lake Erie HAB Seasonal Forecast 2026

americas.alt: Green algal bloom in western Lake Erie seen from satellite, September 20, 2017
americas.credit: Image: NOAA Great Lakes Environmental Research Laboratory (public domain)

americas.sum: Landsat 9 continues a 50-year record of Earth’s land, collecting 740 scenes a day and, with Landsat 8, seeing each place every 8 days.
eli: What is it? The latest Landsat satellite, collecting 740 scenes of Earth each day, almost double its minimum requirement.
Why does it matter? The longest continuous satellite record of Earth’s land surface shows how forests, water and farms change.

How does it help people? Landsat supports water management in drought-prone regions where farms, industry and communities compete for water, and its free data added an estimated $25.6 billion to the U.S. economy in 2023.
americas.alt: Landsat 9 (NASA / USGS) – Earth Observation
places: USGS EROS Center, Sioux Falls, South Dakota (operator and data archive)

americas.sum: A barge-based river cleanup crew that, with more than 141,000 volunteers, has pulled over 14 million pounds of trash from U.S. rivers.
eli: Living Lands & Waters is a team that lives on a big boat called a barge.
They travel down rivers and pick up trash with help from volunteers.
They have picked up more than 14 million pounds of trash and planted millions of trees.

src.name: Living Lands & Waters, Mission and History

americas.alt: Living Lands & Waters – Rivers
americas.credit: Image: NASA/METI/AIST/Japan Space Systems and U.S./Japan ASTER Science Team (PIA23534)

americas.sum: NASA's Lucy is touring asteroids; after Dinkinesh and Donaldjohanson, it reaches its first Trojan asteroid, Eurybates, on 11 August 2027 (NASA).
eli: Lucy is a NASA spacecraft that visits many asteroids , one after another.
Some asteroids travel with Jupiter around the Sun. They are very old.
Studying them is like reading fossils of how the planets were made.
americas.alt: Lucy (NASA) – Planetary Defense

americas.sum: MAAP, an initiative of the nonprofit Amazon Conservation, uses satellite images to report on urgent deforestation and fires in the Amazon.
eli: The Amazon rainforest is huge, and it is hard to see where trees are being cut.
Satellites take pictures from space, and MAAP experts compare them to find new clearings.
Then they publish simple reports so governments and everyone else can act.

src.name: MAAP, Monitoring of the Andes Amazon Program

americas.alt: MAAP, Amazon Deforestation Watch

americas.sum: About 80 species of mangrove trees guard tropical coastlines: their tangled roots hold mud in place, soften storm surges and give fish food and shelter.
eli: What is it? Salt-tolerant coastal forests that grow in low-oxygen, waterlogged soil.
Why does it matter? They protect coastlines from storms and erosion and give fish food and shelter.

src.name: NOAA, What is a mangrove forest?

americas.alt: A young mangrove seedling growing among shoreline rocks at NASA's Kennedy Space Center

americas.sum: The MAR Insurance Programme, run by the nonprofit MAR Fund, uses parametric insurance to pay for fast reef repair after hurricanes along the 1,000 km Mesoamerican Reef.
eli: Hurricanes can smash coral reefs, and repairs only work if they start quickly.
This insurance pays out automatically when winds reach a set speed, with no long wait.
Trained local teams then use the money to fix the reef.

src.name: MAR Fund, The MAR Insurance Programme enters its fifth year (Sept. 2025)

americas.alt: Mesoamerican Reef Insurance Programme (MAR Fund)

americas.sum: Founded by ocean scientist Dr. Sylvia Earle, Mission Blue backs a community-led network of 168 Hope Spots, ocean places local champions work to protect.
eli: A Hope Spot is a special place in the ocean that needs protecting.
People who live nearby pick it and help take care of it.
There are now 168 Hope Spots in 115 countries.
americas.alt: Mission Blue Hope Spots – Ocean

americas.sum: Mote scientists have restored more than 216,000 corals to Florida's Coral Reef, and their restored corals now spawn (Mote figure).
eli: What is it? Coral reef restoration: growing corals and replanting them on the reef.
Why does it matter? Reefs are declining steeply from warming, acidification, disease, pollution and overfishing.
How does it help people? Florida’s Coral Reef provides more than $8 billion in economic impact, attracts visitors and protects coastlines from major storms (Mote figure).

src.name: Mote Marine Laboratory, coral reef restoration

americas.alt: Underwater coral nursery trees growing young corals in the Florida Keys
americas.credit: Image: NOAA Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary (public domain)

americas.sum: Baltimore's Trash Wheels intercept about 500 tons of trash a year before it reaches the harbor and the Chesapeake Bay (organization figure).
eli: What is it? Four trash interceptors that use the current and solar power to lift litter out of the water.
Why does it matter? Stopping trash at the river mouth keeps it out of the harbor, the Chesapeake Bay and the ocean.
americas.alt: Baltimore's harbor on the Patapsco River and the western shore of Chesapeake Bay, seen from Space Shuttle Atlantis

americas.sum: Canada's NEOSSat circles Earth every 100 minutes, scanning near the Sun for asteroids and comets and tracking satellites and debris (CSA).
eli: Some space rocks, called asteroids, pass close to Earth.
NEOSSat is a small Canadian telescope in space that looks for them, even near the Sun.
It also watches satellites and space junk to help avoid crashes in orbit .
americas.alt: NEOSSat Asteroid and Debris Telescope (Canada)
places: Canadian Space Agency headquarters, Longueuil, Quebec

americas.sum: A sailing nonprofit that has pulled more than 850,000 pounds of plastic from the Pacific Gyre in 10 voyages (nonprofit figure).
eli: What is it? Mid-ocean cleanup voyages that recover plastic, from household trash to abandoned fishing nets, then upcycle, recycle and repurpose it.
Why does it matter? Ocean plastic entangles marine life and builds up in the food chain, from plankton to great whales.
How does it help people? Plastic accumulates in the food chain that ends in the seafood people eat; every net and bag pulled out of the gyre stops that cycle (nonprofit description).
americas.alt: Ocean Voyages Institute – Oceans

americas.sum: Since 2014, One Tree Planted has planted more than 171 million trees with 489 partners in 84 countries (organization figure).
eli: One Tree Planted is a group that plants trees all over the world.
They work with local helpers and check on the trees for three years to make sure they grow.
They have planted more than 171 million trees in 84 countries.
americas.alt: Crew planting tree seedlings to restore a wildfire area in Utah's Dixie National Forest
americas.credit: Image: USDA Forest Service Intermountain Region (public domain)

americas.sum: Free satellite data on how much water crops and land use, now for all 48 contiguous states, with more than 13,000 registered users.
eli: Plants drink water and breathe it out into the air.
OpenET uses satellites to measure how much water every field uses.
Farmers can then water only what crops need and save water.
americas.alt: Red circles of irrigated crops near Garden City, Kansas, in a false-color Landsat 7: Circular crop fields around Garden City, Kansas, seen by Landsat

americas.sum: On April 13, 2029, asteroid Apophis passes about 20,000 miles from Earth. NASA's OSIRIS-APEX meets it in June 2029 to see how that close pass changes it.
eli: What is it? An asteroid rendezvous mission studying how a close pass of Earth affects a stony asteroid.
Why does it matter? To learn how asteroids respond to gravity and what they are made of, knowledge that informs planetary defense.
americas.alt: OSIRIS-APEX and Apophis 2029 (NASA)

americas.sum: Two telescopes on Haleakalā, Maui, that in 2021 found nearly as many near-Earth objects as the rest of the world's observatories combined.
eli: Pan-STARRS is two big telescopes on a mountain in Maui.
Their giant cameras photograph the sky to find moving space rocks.
Finding them early keeps Earth safe.

src.name: University of Hawaiʻi, Pan-STARRS search for Near-Earth Objects

americas.sum: Designated in 2025 as America's 18th national marine sanctuary, Papahānaumokuākea covers 582,570 square miles of Pacific Ocean around Hawaiʻi (NOAA).
eli: Far out in the ocean past the main Hawaiian islands is a long chain of tiny islands and reefs.
The United States protects the ocean all around them.
Millions of seabirds nest there, and it is a sacred place for Native Hawaiians.

src.name: USFWS, Midway Atoll National Wildlife Refuge (April 2026)

americas.alt: Papahānaumokuākea National Marine Sanctuary

americas.sum: After two dams came out of Maine's Penobscot River, nearly 5.93 million river herring climbed the Milford fish lift in 2025, up from about 590,000 in 2015.
eli: Dams on the Penobscot River blocked fish from swimming up to lay their eggs.
People took out two dams and built new ways for fish to get past others.
Now millions of fish swim up the river again each year.
americas.alt: Penobscot River Restoration (Maine)
places: Milford Dam fish lift, Penobscot River, Maine

americas.sum: Started by a 9-year-old in 2007, Plant-for-the-Planet trains young Climate Justice Ambassadors and restores forests, including Mexico's Mayan forests.
eli: A 9-year-old boy named Felix asked kids to plant a million trees in every country.
Now more than 100,000 young people have learned to help forests and climate.
The group has planted over 12 million trees in Mexico's Mayan forests.
americas.alt: Students planting red spruce seedlings along the Cherohala Skyway in North Carolina
americas.credit: Image: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service Southeast Region (public domain)

americas.sum: Plastic Bank pays collectors in vulnerable communities to gather ocean-bound plastic, exchanged at local branches for income, food vouchers and school supplies.
eli: What is it? A global bottle-deposit program: collectors in vulnerable communities gather ocean-bound plastic and exchange it at local branches for income, food vouchers, health insurance, and school supplies, all tracked on a blockchain platform.

Why does it matter? Most ocean plastic starts as land-based waste in places with weak waste infrastructure. Making plastic valuable at the source stops it before it enters rivers and the sea, while paying collectors directly.

src.name: Plastic Bank newsletter, June 2026 (all-time data as of June 10, 2026)

americas.sum: Three Canadian radar satellites watch Canada's land, coasts and Arctic day and night, through cloud and smoke, with about 250,000 images a year.
eli: RCM is three satellites that use radar , like a bat uses sound.
Radar works in the dark and sees through clouds and smoke.
It helps ships find safe paths through ice and helps after floods.

src.name: Canadian Space Agency, RADARSAT Constellation Mission FAQ

americas.alt: Swirls of sea ice tracing ocean currents along the coast of Labrador in eastern Canada, photographed from the International Space Station
places: CSA Satellite Operations Control Centre, Longueuil, Quebec

americas.sum: Solar-powered Guardian listening devices and SI detect chainsaws in real time; Rainforest Connection reports more than 726,000 hectares of rainforest protected.
eli: Rainforest Connection puts listening boxes high up in trees.
The boxes use the sun for power and a computer that can tell when it hears a chainsaw.
When it hears one, a ranger gets a message on a phone and can go stop the cutting.
americas.alt: Landsat views of the same patch of Amazon rainforest in Rondônia, Brazil: unbroken forest in 1975 (left) and the fishbone pattern of clearings along roads in 2012 (right)
americas.credit: Image: NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center/Landsat (public domain)

americas.sum: Redonda went from a dusty moonscape to a wildlife haven and is now one of the largest protected areas in the Caribbean (Fauna & Flora).
eli: Redonda is a small island in the Caribbean Sea.
Goats and rats had eaten almost everything, so it was bare rock.
People removed them, and plants and birds came back fast.

src.name: Fauna & Flora, Rejuvenated Redonda granted protected area status (Sept. 2023)

americas.alt: Redonda Island Restoration – Forests
americas.credit: Image: Addshore via Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

americas.sum: A Nevada nonprofit whose ROVs and volunteer divers pull submerged trash from Lake Tahoe, from the surface down to 1,640 feet: over 13 tons in summer 2024 alone.
eli: What is it? A fleet of four ROVs — including the flagship Deep Emerald with a 600-meter fiber optic tether — plus volunteer scuba and free divers, removing submerged debris from Lake Tahoe's depths. They also provide high-resolution underwater surveying photography and videography.

Why does it matter? Lake Tahoe looks pristine from the surface, but abandoned fishing gear, plastic, and debris accumulate below, harming the ecosystem and the lake's legendary clarity. Removing it restores the lake to its original splendor.

americas.sum: In January 2018, Chile and Tompkins Conservation signed the decrees creating a network of new national parks across Patagonia (Tompkins Conservation).
eli: Patagonia is a wild land of mountains, forests and grass at the bottom of South America.
A conservation group bought land and gave it to Chile.
Chile added even more, and together they made new national parks for everyone.

src.name: Tompkins Conservation, Decrees creating 10 million acres of new national parks (29 Jan. 2018)

americas.alt: Route of Parks of Patagonia (Chile)
americas.credit: Image: Gonzalo Lastra via Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)
places: Patagonia National Park, Chacabuco Valley, Chile

americas.sum: Every year about 27.7 million tons of Saharan dust falls on the Amazon, delivering some 22,000 tons of phosphorus that the rainforest needs (NASA).
eli: What is it? Wind carries phosphorus-rich dust from the Sahara across the Atlantic to fertilize the Amazon.
Why does it matter? Rain washes phosphorus out of Amazon soils; the dust replaces it.
How does it help people? A healthy Amazon matters to people far beyond Brazil: its forest helps make its own rain (see The Amazon Makes Its Own Rainy Season), and Saharan dust keeps that forest fed.

src.name: NASA, Saharan dust feeds the Amazon

americas.alt: Saharan Dust Feeds the Amazon – Forests
americas.credit: Image: NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center

americas.sum: The University of South Florida uses NASA satellite data to track the Great Atlantic Sargassum Belt and warn coasts about seaweed blooms (USF).
eli: Sargassum is a brown seaweed that floats in big mats on the ocean.
Some years so much of it washes onto beaches that it piles up on the shore.
Scientists use satellites to see where it is, so coastal towns can get ready.

src.name: USF College of Marine Science, Scientists discover the biggest seaweed bloom in the world (2019)

americas.alt: Sargassum Watch System (USF) – Ocean
americas.credit: Image: Contains modified Copernicus Sentinel-2 data, processed by ESA
places: USF College of Marine Science, St. Petersburg, Florida

americas.sum: NOAA's SARSAT satellites relay distress beacon signals to rescuers; the international system has supported more than 50,000 rescues worldwide since 1982 (NOAA).
eli: Boats, planes and hikers can carry a small emergency beacon.
If they are in trouble, the beacon sends a signal that satellites hear.
The satellites tell rescuers where to go, and that has saved thousands of people.
americas.alt: Personal locator beacons that send distress signals to COSPAS-SARSAT satellites
places: U.S. SARSAT Mission Control Center, Suitland, Maryland (NOAA)

americas.sum: Sea Turtle Conservancy works in 8 countries, has tagged and monitored more than 550 turtles and trained over 1,200 researchers (nonprofit figures).
eli: Sea turtles are ancient animals that swim across whole oceans.
Sea Turtle Conservancy protects the beaches where they lay their eggs.
It also tracks turtles with satellites to learn where they go.
americas.alt: Sea Turtle Conservancy – Oceans

americas.sum: SeaTrees connects people with local partners restoring mangroves, coral reefs, kelp forests and seagrass meadows around the world (SeaTrees).
eli: "Seatrees" are ocean plants like mangroves , kelp and seagrass .
SeaTrees helps people plant and protect them with help from local teams.
These plants give fish a home and protect beaches from big storms.
americas.alt: A restoration worker places repotted mangrove seedlings in a marshy channel at Kennedy Space Center

americas.sum: SMAP maps the water in Earth's soil from space, helping improve predictions of weather, floods and droughts (NASA).
eli: SMAP is a satellite that measures how wet or dry the ground is.
It can also tell if the soil is frozen or thawed.
This helps farmers and scientists get ready for floods and droughts.
americas.alt: Artist's rendering of NASA's SMAP satellite scanning a wide strip of Earth's surface
places: NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory, Pasadena, California

americas.sum: Surfrider Foundation volunteers protect the ocean, waves and beaches, and in 2025 they removed 338,383 pounds of trash from U.S. coasts (Surfrider).
eli: Surfrider is a group of people who love the beach and want it clean.
Volunteers pick up trash so it doesn't hurt sea animals.
They also count what they find to help stop plastic at the source.
americas.alt: Two surfers at sunset among sea stacks and crashing waves at Second Beach in Olympic Coast National Marine Sanctuary
americas.credit: Image: Matt McIntosh/NOAA (public domain)

americas.sum: SWOT measures more than 95% of Earth's lakes larger than 15 acres and rivers wider than 330 feet, the first global survey of fresh water.
eli: What is it? A radar interferometer satellite that measures the height of water on land and at sea.
Why does it matter? Fresh water is unevenly measured on the ground; SWOT gives every country the same view of its rivers and lakes.
americas.alt: SWOT (NASA–CNES) – Earth Observation

americas.sum: From geostationary orbit, NASA's TEMPO measures air pollution over North America every daylight hour, a first from space (NASA).
eli: TEMPO is a space tool that checks how dirty the air is.
It stays above the same spot on Earth and looks at North America every hour while the sun is up.
This helps warn people on bad air days so they can stay safe.
americas.alt: NASA TEMPO map of nitrogen dioxide air pollution over North America, highest over big cities
americas.credit: Image: NASA's Scientific Visualization Studio (public domain)
places: Smithsonian Astrophysical Observatory, Cambridge, Massachusetts (mission lead)

americas.sum: Terraformation grows native, biodiverse forests from seed to canopy across the tropics and Hawaii, funding seed collection, nurseries, planting and monitoring.
eli: What is it? Restoring degraded land into native, biodiverse forests that capture carbon and support communities. Projects use up to five times more native species than typical carbon-offset plantings, tracked with open-source software from nursery to canopy.

Why does it matter? Half of global forests are damaged or destroyed. Native, biodiverse restoration rebuilds habitat and resilience far better than monoculture planting, and long-term stewardship is what makes the carbon capture last.
americas.alt: Terraformation native forest

americas.n: The Amazon Makes Its Own Rainy Season
americas.sum: Water breathed out by Amazon trees starts the rainy season two to three months before winds alone would bring it (NASA JPL).
eli: What is it? Transpiration: trees pull water from the ground and release vapor that builds rain clouds.
Why does it matter? The finding helps explain why deforestation in this region is linked with reduced rainfall.

How does it help people? Losing a major Amazonian forest ecosystem could increase Brazilian droughts and potentially disrupt rainfall as far away as Texas, so keeping the forest standing protects water for people.

src.name: NASA JPL, the Amazon makes its own rainy season

americas.alt: The Amazon Makes Its Own Rainy Season

americas.sum: The Ocean Cleanup removes legacy plastic from ocean garbage patches and intercepts it in rivers: more than 65 million kilograms caught as of October 2026.
eli: What is it? Two fronts: large floating systems that extract legacy plastic from ocean garbage patches, and solar-powered Interceptors that catch plastic in rivers before it reaches the sea.
Why does it matter? Plastic harms marine wildlife, breaks into microplastics , and persists for decades. Cleanup protects the water we depend on.
americas.alt: The Ocean Cleanup – Oceans
americas.credit: Created by SI and Biological SI Partner

americas.sum: Deep-ocean buoys, satellites, GPS signals and seafloor cables spot tsunamis in the open ocean so coastal communities get time to reach high ground (NOAA, NASA).
eli: A tsunami is a group of giant waves, usually made when a big earthquake shakes the sea floor.
Buoys, satellites and special computers watch the ocean and tell warning centers when a tsunami is coming.
If the ground shakes hard or the sea pulls back fast near a beach, go to high ground right away.

src.name: NASA, SWOT satellite measures tsunami after massive quake

americas.alt: The Science of Tsunami Detection
places: Pacific Tsunami Warning Center, Ford Island, Hawaii (NOAA)
National Tsunami Warning Center, Palmer, Alaska (NOAA)

americas.sum: Partnering with East African farmers on regenerative farms: 450M+ trees grown and 99,000 acres restored (nonprofit figures).
eli: What is it? Regenerative farming with diverse trees and plants to restore soil, biodiversity and harvests.
Why does it matter? Degraded land hurts families; restored soil means more food and income.
How does it help people? Farmers and their families are the first to benefit: restored soil equals more food, and more food creates a surplus to sell (nonprofit description).
americas.alt: The Tana River winding across the land in Kenya, seen by the Copernicus Sentinel-2 satellite
americas.credit: Image: contains modified Copernicus Sentinel data (2020), processed by ESA (CC BY-SA 3.0 IGO)

americas.sum: Trout Unlimited restores and reconnects cold, clean rivers, reconnecting 1,052 miles of streams in its 2024-25 season (Trout Unlimited).
eli: Trout and salmon need cold, clean rivers to live.
Trout Unlimited fixes damaged streams and removes things that block fish.
More than 20,000 volunteers help care for rivers.
americas.alt: A male coaster brook trout with orange belly and spotted sides, reared at Iron River National Fish Hatchery in Wisconsin
americas.credit: Image: Katie Steiger-Meister/USFWS (public domain)

americas.sum: Waterkeeper Alliance unites hundreds of local Waterkeeper groups that patrol and protect more than 6 million square miles of rivers, lakes and coastlines.
eli: A Waterkeeper is a person or group who watches over a river, lake or coast.
They check the water and stop people from polluting it.
It all started with fishermen who saved the Hudson River in New York.

americas.sum: How the James Webb Space Telescope tracked asteroid 2024 YR4 in February 2026 and ruled out a 2032 Moon impact, two years before ground telescopes could.
eli: What is it? Asteroid 2024 YR4, about 60 meters across, was briefly the most dangerous asteroid found in 20 years. Earth impact was soon ruled out, but a roughly 4% chance of hitting the Moon on December 22, 2032 remained (NASA's last estimate was 4.3%).
Why does it matter? A lunar impact of this scale could affect satellites and future astronauts around the Moon. Knowing years early removes that worry, and proves a technique we can reuse.

src.name: ESA, 2024 YR4 will not impact the Moon

americas.alt: Webb and Asteroid 2024 YR4: The Moon Is Safe
places: Space Telescope Science Institute, Baltimore (Webb mission operations)

americas.sum: Gray wolves returned to Yellowstone in 1995 after nearly 70 years; in January 2026 at least 84 lived in the park, in eight packs (NPS).
eli: Wolves disappeared from Yellowstone National Park for almost 70 years.
In 1995, people brought wolves back.
Scientists now study how wolves, elk and other animals live together again.

src.name: National Park Service, Wolf management in Yellowstone

americas.alt: Yellowstone Wolves – Forests

eurafrica.sum: The Environment Agency – Abu Dhabi tracks more than 18.5 million mangroves planted across over 1,775 hectares with its new Mangrove Observatory.
eli: Mangroves are trees that grow in salty water along the coast.
Abu Dhabi is planting millions of them to bring its coastal forests back.
A new website uses satellites and field checks to see how many really grow.

src.name: Abu Dhabi Media Office, EAD launches Mangrove Observatory (July 2026)

eurafrica.alt: Abu Dhabi Mangrove Restoration
places: Abu Dhabi coast, United Arab Emirates

eurafrica.sum: African Parks manages 24 protected areas in 13 countries, covering over 20 million hectares, in partnership with governments and local communities (nonprofit).
eli: Some of Africa's national parks were losing their animals because there was not enough money or care.
African Parks works with each country's government to run those parks well.
It brings back animals that had disappeared and helps the people who live nearby.
eurafrica.alt: African Parks – Forests

eurafrica.sum: On 18 September 2026, Norway's government created the Andfjorden Marine Protected Area across Andøy, Harstad and Senja (Norwegian government).
eli: Andfjorden is a big, cold stretch of sea in the far north of Norway.
Under the water there are coral reefs, kelp forests and lots of fish, whales and seabirds.
Norway made it a protected area, with extra-strict rules in the most fragile spots.

src.name: Norwegian Ministry of Climate and Environment, Andfjorden becomes Norway's largest marine protected area (18 Sept. 2026)

eurafrica.alt: Andfjorden Marine Protected Area (Norway)
eurafrica.credit: Image: Ryan Hodnett via Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)
places: Andfjorden, between Andøya and Senja, Norway

eurafrica.n: ATLAS Asteroid Terrestrial-impact Last Alert System
eurafrica.sum: Four robotic telescopes, two in Hawaiʻi, search the entire dark sky every 24 hours for asteroids that could hit Earth, so people can be warned.
eli: ATLAS is four robot telescopes that scan the night sky.
They look for space rocks that come close to Earth.
An early warning gives people time to get ready or move away.

src.name: NASA, ATLAS now capable of full-sky search

eurafrica.alt: The island of Hawaiʻi, home of Mauna Loa, seen from the International Space Station

eurafrica.sum: Since 1994, Jordan's Royal Society for the Conservation of Nature has been restoring the Azraq wetland in the eastern desert (RSCN).
eli: Azraq is an oasis, a wet place in the middle of a desert in Jordan.
People pumped out so much water that it almost dried up.
Conservationists brought water back to pools and returned a tiny fish found nowhere else.

src.name: World Wetlands Day (Ramsar), Restoration of the Azraq Wetland, Jordan (May 2021)

eurafrica.alt: Azraq Wetland Reserve Restoration (Jordan)
eurafrica.credit: Image: Mohammad hajeer via Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

eurafrica.sum: ESA's Biomass satellite, launched April 29, 2025, carries the first P-band radar in space, seeing through forest canopies to measure the carbon stored in trees.
eli: What is it? The first P-band synthetic aperture radar in space.
Why does it matter? To measure the woody biomass where forests store carbon, and track deforestation and regrowth.
eurafrica.alt: Biomass (ESA) – Earth Observation

eurafrica.sum: CHIME will image Earth in more than 200 colours of light to support sustainable farming, food security and biodiversity (ESA).
eli: CHIME will be two satellites that see far more colours than our eyes can.
Those colours show how healthy crops and soils are.
Farmers and scientists can use this to grow food and protect nature.
eurafrica.alt: Patchwork of farm fields in Montana's Golden Triangle, seen by Landsat
eurafrica.credit: Image: NASA Earth Observatory/Lauren Dauphin, Landsat data from USGS (public domain)

eurafrica.sum: Three spacecraft will wait in space for a fresh comet and fly past it together to make a 3D map; launch is planned for late 2028 or early 2029 (ESA).
eli: Some comets come from very far away and have never been near the Sun before.
Comet Interceptor will wait in space until scientists find one.
Then three spacecraft fly past it together to make a 3D picture.
eurafrica.alt: Comet Interceptor (ESA / JAXA)

eurafrica.sum: Europe's air monitoring service forecasts air pollution, smoke and dust worldwide twice a day for more than 23,500 users, free and open.
eli: CAMS checks the air all over the world, from smoke to dust to pollution.
It uses satellites and computer models to forecast dirty air days ahead.
People can plan to stay safe on bad air days.

src.name: Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service, About us

eurafrica.alt: Smoke from fires on Sumatra blowing toward Malaysia and Singapore, seen by NASA's Aqua satellite

eurafrica.n: Copernicus CO2M Carbon Dioxide Monitoring (ESA / EU)
eurafrica.sum: A planned trio of satellites that will measure the carbon dioxide and methane people release, so countries can check whether their emission cuts are working.
eli: Some gases, like carbon dioxide , trap heat and warm our planet.
CO2M will be three satellites that measure how much of these gases people release.
That helps countries see if their plans to cut pollution are working.

src.name: ESA, Europe’s carbon dioxide monitoring mission elevated to the power of three

eurafrica.alt: Artist's view of a Copernicus CO2M satellite in orbit measuring carbon dioxide from human activity
eurafrica.credit: Image: ESA/Mlabspace (CC BY-SA 3.0 IGO)

eurafrica.sum: Free, open ocean data and forecasts for the whole planet. In 2025 users downloaded almost 15,000 terabytes of ocean data from Copernicus Marine.
eli: Copernicus Marine is like a weather service for the ocean.
It shows ocean temperature, currents, sea ice and tiny plant life.
Sailors, scientists and fishers use it for free.
eurafrica.alt: Swirls of a phytoplankton bloom in the deep blue central North Atlantic Ocean, seen by satellite
eurafrica.credit: Image: NASA/GSFC/Jeff Schmaltz/MODIS Land Rapid Response Team

eurafrica.sum: Sentinel-1 radar sees through clouds, day and night, to map floods, earthquakes and ice; Sentinel-1C and 1D joined in 2024 and 2025.
eli: What is it? Radar satellites imaging Earth through cloud and darkness.
Why does it matter? Continuous radar imagery for disaster response, ice, land and ocean monitoring.
eurafrica.alt: Copernicus Sentinel-1 (ESA)

eurafrica.sum: From geostationary orbit on MTG-S1, Sentinel-4 measures air pollution such as nitrogen dioxide and ozone over Europe and North Africa every hour (ESA).
eli: Sentinel-4 is a space tool that watches the air over Europe.
It stays above the same spot and checks the air every hour.
This helps warn people when the air is dirty.
eurafrica.alt: Europe and North Africa seen by Copernicus Sentinel-4 from geostationary orbit
eurafrica.credit: Image: contains modified Copernicus Sentinel data (2025), processed by ESA (CC BY-SA 3.0 IGO)
places: EUMETSAT, Darmstadt, Germany (operates MTG-S1, which carries Sentinel-4)

eurafrica.sum: Copernicus Sentinel-5P maps the gases in the air we breathe, covering the whole planet every day with its Tropomi instrument (ESA).
eli: Sentinel-5P is a satellite that sniffs the air from space.
Every day it checks the whole planet for gases that make air dirty.
This helps keep people healthy and track gases that warm Earth.
eurafrica.alt: World map of average nitrogen dioxide pollution in 2014 measured from space by the Ozone Monitoring Instrument on NASA's Aura satellite, brightest over big cities and industrial areas
eurafrica.credit: Image: NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center (public domain)

eurafrica.sum: Digital Earth Africa turns satellite data into free and open maps of water, farmland and coasts for the whole African continent (Digital Earth Africa).
eli: Satellites take pictures of Africa all the time, but the raw data is hard to use.
Digital Earth Africa cleans it up and turns it into ready-made maps.
Anyone can use them for free to track water, crops and coastlines.
eurafrica.alt: Digital Earth Africa – Earth Observation
places: icipe, Nairobi, Kenya (host of the programme)

eurafrica.sum: Eden: People+Planet restores landscapes with local communities, including a 394,000-hectare project in Tanzania's Rubeho Mountains (Eden).
eli: Eden helps people bring back forests and wild land near their homes.
In Tanzania, people from 40 villages are helping protect a huge mountain area.
Healthy forests keep water clean and give animals a place to live.
eurafrica.alt: Mount Kilimanjaro and the surrounding highlands in Tanzania, seen from the Space Shuttle

eurafrica.sum: Europe's wildfire system forecasts fire danger and maps burnt areas from satellites. In 2024 it mapped wildfires in 42 countries.
eli: EFFIS warns when the weather makes forest fires likely.
After a fire, satellites show exactly how much land burned.
Countries use this to fight fires and plan how forests recover.
eurafrica.alt: Smoke from wildfires near the southern coast of Portugal, photographed from the International Space Station
places: European Commission Joint Research Centre, Ispra, Italy

eurafrica.sum: Earth Fire Alliance's FireSat satellites are built to spot wildfires as small as 5 by 5 meters from space and get the data to firefighters fast.
eli: Wildfires are much easier to stop while they are still small.
FireSat satellites carry special cameras that can sense heat from space.
They can spot a fire about the size of two parking spaces and help firefighters act fast.

src.name: Earth Fire Alliance, FireSat first light (Sep 16, 2026)

eurafrica.alt: FireSat (Earth Fire Alliance)

eurafrica.sum: By thinning small trees, forest elephants help central Africa's rainforests store more carbon: 26 to 60 more tonnes of biomass per hectare (Nature Geoscience).
eli: Forest elephants live in the rainforests of central and West Africa.
As they walk and eat, they push over and munch small trees.
That leaves room for big, heavy trees that store more carbon.
eurafrica.alt: Forest Elephants, Carbon Gardeners
places: Brazzaville, Republic of Congo (WCS Congo, forest elephant program)

eurafrica.sum: FreshWater Watch trains citizen scientists to test rivers, lakes and ponds: 80,000+ datasets from 22,000+ volunteers (organization figures).
eli: Rivers and lakes can get dirty in ways you cannot see.
FreshWater Watch gives people simple test kits to check the water.
Scientists and governments use the results to find problems and fix them.
eurafrica.alt: A U.S. Geological Survey scientist collecting a water sample from the Mississippi River at Baton Rouge
eurafrica.credit: Image: Scott Dennis/USGS (public domain)

eurafrica.sum: Europe's Galileo is the world's most precise satellite navigation system, serving over five billion smartphone users and helping rescues (ESA).
eli: Galileo is a group of satellites that tells your phone exactly where it is.
Each satellite has very accurate atomic clocks.
Galileo satellites can also hear emergency beacons and pass the alert to rescuers.

src.name: ESA, Two new Galileo satellites enter service

eurafrica.alt: A Galileo navigation satellite inside ESA's acoustic test chamber in the Netherlands
eurafrica.credit: Image: ESA-Anneke Le Floc'h (CC BY-SA 3.0 IGO)

eurafrica.sum: The Mozambique government and the Gorongosa Project are restoring Gorongosa National Park as "a park for the people" (Gorongosa).
eli: Gorongosa is a big wildlife park in Mozambique, in Africa.
Rangers, scientists and local people work together to protect it.
The latest count found more big animals there than ever recorded.

src.name: Stalmans & Peel, Aerial wildlife count of Gorongosa National Park, October 2024

eurafrica.alt: Gorongosa National Park Restoration
eurafrica.credit: Image: Judy Gallagher via Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 2.0)

eurafrica.sum: An African-led effort to restore land across the Sahel. A 2020 UN status report counted about 4 million hectares restored inside the Great Green Wall zone.
eli: The Sahara desert is next to a dry area called the Sahel.
Many African countries are planting and protecting trees and grass there.
They want to make a long green belt across Africa.
eurafrica.alt: Great Green Wall (African Union / UNCCD)

eurafrica.sum: Volunteer divers recover ghost nets: Healthy Seas reports 1,309.1 tons of nets and marine litter removed since 2013 (Healthy Seas figure).
eli: What is it? Cleanups that remove ghost nets and other marine litter, plus recycling of suitable nets into ECONYL® yarn with Aquafil.
Why does it matter? Ghost nets stay in the sea for hundreds of years and keep catching and killing marine life.
How does it help people? Healthy Seas works with fishing communities and fish farmers to prevent net loss and turns recovered nylon into new yarn, creating value from waste (nonprofit description).
eurafrica.alt: Divers in an inflatable boat hauling in derelict fishing nets removed from the reefs of Papahānaumokuākea Marine National Monument

eurafrica.sum: ESA's Hera arrives at the asteroid Dimorphos in November 2026 to measure what NASA's DART impact did, turning deflection into a repeatable defense.
eli: What is it? A small, van-sized deep-space spacecraft that will perform a close-up "crash scene investigation" of Dimorphos, measuring its mass, its shifted orbit and DART's impact crater. Juventas will make the first radar sounding inside an asteroid .
Why does it matter? To turn DART's one-off hit into a well-understood, repeatable technique for defending Earth from hazardous asteroids, by measuring how much push the impact really delivered.
eurafrica.alt: Hera: Investigating the Asteroid DART Moved
eurafrica.credit: Image: ESA – Science Office (CC BY-SA 3.0 IGO, resized)

eurafrica.sum: ESA's first Scout mission uses reflected navigation-satellite signals to measure soil moisture, wetlands and frozen ground (ESA).
eli: Navigation satellites send signals that bounce off the ground.
HydroGNSS catches those echoes to tell how wet the soil is.
That helps farmers, flood planners and scientists watch Earth's water.
eurafrica.alt: NASA SMAP world map of surface soil moisture, August 25-27, 2015

eurafrica.sum: With farmers and pastoralists in Africa, Justdiggit is restoring 525,000 hectares of dry land and has brought back 32.3 million trees (organization figures).
eli: In some dry places, rain runs off the hard ground instead of soaking in.
Justdiggit helps people dig little smile-shaped holes that catch the rain.
Then grass grows back, the land turns green, and the planet cools down.
eurafrica.alt: Southeast Kenya seen by the Copernicus Sentinel-2 satellite, green vegetation along the coast and drier land inland
eurafrica.credit: Image: contains modified Copernicus Sentinel data (2023), processed by ESA

eurafrica.sum: Treatment plants that remove phosphorus brought Lake Constance back to the clear state typical of Alpine lakes (International Commission for the Protection of Lake…
eli: Lake Constance sits between Germany, Austria and Switzerland.
Too much phosphorus from wastewater made algae grow, which is bad for the lake.
The countries built treatment plants that take out phosphorus, and the lake recovered.
eurafrica.alt: Lake Constance Phosphorus Recovery
places: Lake Constance (Bodensee), Germany, Austria and Switzerland

eurafrica.sum: Life Terra and its partners have planted more than 36 million trees across Europe (company figure), working toward a goal of 500 million trees.
eli: What is it? Community-based tree planting paired with an app and monitoring technology that registers every tree and tracks its growth. They run large professional plantings, local volunteer events, school climate education, and corporate tree-adoption programs.

Why does it matter? Europe needs massive reforestation to meet climate targets, and trees only deliver if they survive. Monitoring plus long-term landowner commitment turns planting events into permanent forests.

src.name: Life Terra press release via EURACTIV PR, May 13, 2026

eurafrica.alt: Life Terra tree planting

eurafrica.sum: Since 1998, the Global Nature Fund's Living Lakes Network has protected and restored lakes and wetlands with 130 member organizations in more than 60 countries.
eli: Living Lakes is a team of groups that look after lakes all over the world.
They clean up trash and help people near lakes earn money without harming nature.
In Mongolia they help protect a lake that is about 2 million years old.

eurafrica.sum: London's new super sewer catches sewage that used to spill into the River Thames in storms, with room for 1.6 million cubic metres (Tideway).
eli: When it rains hard in London, old sewers used to overflow into the River Thames.
A giant new tunnel under the river now catches that dirty water.
The water is sent away to be cleaned, so the river stays healthier.
eurafrica.alt: London Tideway Tunnel (Super Sewer)
places: Abbey Mills Pumping Station, East London

eurafrica.sum: The UN's satellite methane alert system has sent more than 3,500 alerts about major leaks in 33 countries, and responses rose from 1% to 12% in a year.
eli: Methane is a gas that heats the planet, and big leaks can be seen from space.
The United Nations watches satellite data and tells countries and companies about leaks.
When they fix a leak, the air gets cleaner and the planet heats up less.

src.name: UNEP IMEO, Methane Alert and Response System

eurafrica.alt: A cluster of methane plumes detected from orbit in southern Uzbekistan, shown in color over a satellite map

eurafrica.sum: Rangers, vets and communities in Uganda, Rwanda and the DR Congo pulled mountain gorillas up from Critically Endangered (IUCN).
eli: Mountain gorillas live in misty forests on volcanoes in Africa.
Hunting traps and diseases had made them very rare.
Rangers removed traps and vets cared for them, and now there are more.

src.name: Greater Virunga Transboundary Collaboration, Bwindi-Sarambwe census press release (Dec. 2019)

eurafrica.alt: Mountain Gorilla Recovery – Forests
eurafrica.credit: Image: Diego Delso via Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

eurafrica.sum: Europe's asteroid watch centre computes orbits and impact risks every day and keeps a public list of every asteroid with a non-zero chance of hitting Earth.
eli: Some asteroids pass near Earth, and scientists need to know where they will go.
ESA's centre in Italy collects telescope data and works out their paths.
If an asteroid ever looks dangerous, they warn emergency teams.
eurafrica.alt: A sequence of radar images of the binary asteroid 2011 UL21 and its small moon

eurafrica.n: Okavango Delta: The River That Ends in a Desert
eurafrica.sum: The Okavango Delta in Botswana is a near-pristine inland delta whose waters drain into the Kalahari sands instead of the sea (UNESCO).
eli: The Okavango River flows into Botswana but never reaches the ocean.
Every year its water spreads out across the desert, right in the dry season.
Elephants, lions and birds gather to drink and feed in the new wetland.

src.name: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Okavango Delta

eurafrica.alt: Okavango Delta: The River That Ends in a Desert
eurafrica.credit: Image: Diego Delso via Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

eurafrica.sum: Plastic Bank pays collectors in vulnerable communities to gather ocean-bound plastic, exchanged at local branches for income, food vouchers and school supplies.
eli: What is it? A global bottle-deposit program: collectors in vulnerable communities gather ocean-bound plastic and exchange it at local branches for income, food vouchers, health insurance, and school supplies, all tracked on a blockchain platform.

Why does it matter? Most ocean plastic starts as land-based waste in places with weak waste infrastructure. Making plastic valuable at the source stops it before it enters rivers and the sea, while paying collectors directly.

src.name: Plastic Bank newsletter, June 2026 (all-time data as of June 10, 2026)

eurafrica.sum: Plastic Odyssey sets up small recycling factories in places with no recycling system, turning plastic waste into useful products and local jobs.
eli: In many places there is nowhere to recycle plastic, so it ends up in the sea.
Plastic Odyssey helps people build small recycling factories.
They turn old plastic into useful things, like paving stones, and create jobs.
eurafrica.alt: A team pulling a giant tangled mass of washed-up fishing nets across the beach of Lisianski Island in Papahānaumokuākea Marine National Monument

eurafrica.sum: The Mediterranean seagrass Posidonia oceanica forms meadows that are thousands of years old and store carbon in the seafloor (CEAB-CSIC).
eli: Posidonia is a sea grass that grows under the Mediterranean Sea.
Some patches have been growing for more than 2,000 years.
They hold carbon in the sand and give baby fish a safe home.

src.name: CEAB-CSIC, The Illetes Posidonia meadow is over 2,000 years old

eurafrica.alt: Posidonia Seagrass Meadows – Ocean

eurafrica.sum: Project Seagrass, a UK charity, has planted more than 150,000 seagrass seeds to bring back underwater meadows (organization figures).
eli: Seagrass is a real plant with flowers that grows underwater near the coast.
Its meadows give baby fish a safe home and keep the water clean.
Project Seagrass plants seagrass seeds to grow the meadows back.
eurafrica.alt: Project Seagrass – Ocean

eurafrica.sum: Solar-powered Guardian listening devices and SI detect chainsaws in real time; Rainforest Connection reports more than 726,000 hectares of rainforest protected.
eli: Rainforest Connection puts listening boxes high up in trees.
The boxes use the sun for power and a computer that can tell when it hears a chainsaw.
When it hears one, a ranger gets a message on a phone and can go stop the cutting.
eurafrica.alt: Landsat views of the same patch of Amazon rainforest in Rondônia, Brazil: unbroken forest in 1975 (left) and the fishbone pattern of clearings along roads in 2012 (right)
eurafrica.credit: Image: NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center/Landsat (public domain)

eurafrica.sum: ESA and JAXA's Ramses must launch by spring 2028 to meet Apophis before its 2029 Earth pass. Its €81.2 million build contract was signed in February 2026.
eli: What is it? A spacecraft with two CubeSats that will study Apophis before, during and after its Earth pass.
Why does it matter? To understand asteroids ' physical properties and behaviour and strengthen planetary defense.
eurafrica.alt: Ramses (ESA / JAXA) – Planetary Defense

eurafrica.sum: Rewilding Europe helps wild nature come back across Europe. Rewilding Europe, working with local partners in large pioneering landscapes.
eli: Rewilding means letting nature take care of itself again.
Rewilding Europe helps bring back big animals like bison, which keep forests and meadows healthy.
People can visit these wild places, which helps the villages nearby.
eurafrica.alt: Rewilding Europe – Forests

eurafrica.sum: At 34 locations, the Netherlands widened floodplains and dug side channels so rivers can safely carry more water (Rijkswaterstaat).
eli: When rivers get very full, they can flood towns.
The Netherlands moved dikes back and dug extra channels so the water has more room.
Now high water can spread out safely, and the riverside landscape is better too.
eurafrica.alt: Room for the River (Netherlands)
places: Deventer, on the IJssel, one of the Room for the River sites

eurafrica.sum: Every year about 27.7 million tons of Saharan dust falls on the Amazon, delivering some 22,000 tons of phosphorus that the rainforest needs (NASA).
eli: What is it? Wind carries phosphorus-rich dust from the Sahara across the Atlantic to fertilize the Amazon.
Why does it matter? Rain washes phosphorus out of Amazon soils; the dust replaces it.
How does it help people? A healthy Amazon matters to people far beyond Brazil: its forest helps make its own rain (see The Amazon Makes Its Own Rainy Season), and Saharan dust keeps that forest fed.

src.name: NASA, Saharan dust feeds the Amazon

eurafrica.alt: Saharan Dust Feeds the Amazon – Forests
eurafrica.credit: Image: NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center

eurafrica.sum: SeaTrees connects people with local partners restoring mangroves, coral reefs, kelp forests and seagrass meadows around the world (SeaTrees).
eli: "Seatrees" are ocean plants like mangroves , kelp and seagrass .
SeaTrees helps people plant and protect them with help from local teams.
These plants give fish a home and protect beaches from big storms.
eurafrica.alt: A restoration worker places repotted mangrove seedlings in a marshy channel at Kennedy Space Center

eurafrica.n: Seychelles Marine Spatial Plan and Debt-for-Nature Swap
eurafrica.sum: Seychelles turned a debt-for-nature swap with The Nature Conservancy into a plan that protects 30% of its waters (State House Seychelles).
eli: Seychelles is a country made of islands in the Indian Ocean.
It made a deal: part of its debt was refinanced to pay for ocean protection.
Now almost a third of its sea is protected, bigger than Germany.

src.name: State House Seychelles, Seychelles designates 30% of its EEZ as Marine Protected Area (26 March 2020)

eurafrica.alt: Seychelles Marine Spatial Plan and Debt-for-Nature Swap
eurafrica.credit: Image: Ron Van Oers/UNESCO via Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 3.0 IGO)

eurafrica.sum: SWOT measures more than 95% of Earth's lakes larger than 15 acres and rivers wider than 330 feet, the first global survey of fresh water.
eli: What is it? A radar interferometer satellite that measures the height of water on land and at sea.
Why does it matter? Fresh water is unevenly measured on the ground; SWOT gives every country the same view of its rivers and lakes.
eurafrica.alt: SWOT (NASA–CNES) – Earth Observation

eurafrica.sum: Captive breeding and reintroductions brought the Arabian oryx back, with about 1,000 in the wild by 2011 (IUCN).
eli: The Arabian oryx is a white desert antelope with long, straight horns.
Hunters shot the last wild one in 1972.
Zoos bred them and set them free again, and now about 1,000 live in the wild.

src.name: IUCN, A grain of hope in the desert (June 2011)

eurafrica.alt: The Arabian Oryx Comeback – Forests
eurafrica.credit: Image: Charles J. Sharp via Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 3.0)
places: Arabian Peninsula, home range of the Arabian oryx

eurafrica.sum: The Great Bubble Barrier's bubble curtain guides plastic out of Amsterdam's canals into a catchment across the full width and depth, while boats and fish pass.
eli: What is it? A perforated tube on the riverbed pumps air into a diagonal curtain of bubbles. The rising current lifts plastic to the surface and the flow carries it into a catchment system. Their FAQ says it targets plastic from 1 mm to 1 m and cites an 86 percent catch rate for floating plastic.
Why does it matter? Boats and fish can pass. The screen runs 24/7 across the full width and depth, including plastic below the surface that a boat crew can miss.

eurafrica.sum: Spain and Portugal brought the Iberian lynx back from the edge: the 2025 census counted 2,663, almost double 2021 (MITECO).
eli: The Iberian lynx is a wild cat that lives only in Spain and Portugal.
By 2002 there were fewer than 100 left.
Breeding, releases and protection helped, and now there are more than 2,600.

src.name: MITECO, Iberian lynx population reached 2,663 in 2025 (June 2026)

eurafrica.alt: The Iberian Lynx Comeback – Forests
eurafrica.credit: Image: Diego Delso via Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)
places: Almuradiel, Ciudad Real, Spain, in lynx country

eurafrica.sum: The Ocean Cleanup removes legacy plastic from ocean garbage patches and intercepts it in rivers: more than 65 million kilograms caught as of October 2026.
eli: What is it? Two fronts: large floating systems that extract legacy plastic from ocean garbage patches, and solar-powered Interceptors that catch plastic in rivers before it reaches the sea.
Why does it matter? Plastic harms marine wildlife, breaks into microplastics , and persists for decades. Cleanup protects the water we depend on.
eurafrica.alt: The Ocean Cleanup – Oceans
eurafrica.credit: Created by SI and Biological SI Partner

eurafrica.n: Trees for Life: Restoring the Caledonian Forest
eurafrica.sum: Trees for Life is rewilding the Scottish Highlands, bringing back the Caledonian forest, of which less than 2% survives (Trees for Life).
eli: The Caledonian forest of pine trees once covered much of the Scottish Highlands.
Today only small pieces are left.
Volunteers plant trees and protect young ones, so the wild forest can grow back.
eurafrica.alt: Trees for Life: Restoring the Caledonian Forest
eurafrica.credit: Image: Chris via Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 2.0)

eurafrica.sum: WeForest has grown more than 118 million trees and has 100,000 hectares of forest under restoration and conservation (WeForest).
eli: WeForest helps whole areas of land grow back into healthy forests.
It works with local families so trees and people can both thrive.
It has grown more than 118 million trees so far.
eurafrica.alt: A tree seedling being planted on the Sioux Ranger District of Custer Gallatin National Forest
eurafrica.credit: Image: USDA Forest Service (public domain)

asiaoceania.sum: 4ocean removes plastic from oceans, rivers, and coastlines with full-time cleanup crews, funded by products made from recovered plastic.
eli: What is it? Full-time professional captains and cleanup crews recover plastic and trash from oceans, rivers, and coastlines every day. The model: each bracelet or product sold funds the removal of one pound of trash, and recovered material is sorted, shredded, and turned into recycled products.

Why does it matter? Plastic harms marine wildlife, breaks into microplastics , and persists for decades. 4ocean's founders saw beaches buried in garbage on a surf trip to Bali in 2015 and built a business that pays crews to remove it every day.
asiaoceania.credit: Created by SI and Biological SI Partner

asiaoceania.n: Atoll Rewilding: Seabirds Against Sea-Level Rise
asiaoceania.sum: A 2026 study of 28 atoll islands found that removing rats and restoring native plants boosts the seabirds, reefs and sand that help atolls keep up with rising seas.
eli: Atolls are rings of tiny, low islands made by coral.
Seabirds catch fish at sea and leave droppings full of nutrients on the islands, which wash onto the reef.
Where rats are gone, birds come back, reefs grow faster and the islands get more sand to stay above the waves.

src.name: Graham, Benkwitt et al., Seabirds and native vegetation drive ecosystem processes that support atoll island resilience, Science Advances (14 Oct. 2026)

asiaoceania.alt: Atoll Rewilding: Seabirds Against Sea-Level Rise
asiaoceania.credit: Image: NASA Johnson Space Center, ISS crew photo ISS018-E-024351
places: Tetiaroa atoll, French Polynesia, one of the study sites

asiaoceania.sum: Seoul removed an ageing road and elevated motorway that covered the Cheonggyecheon stream and restored it along a 5.84 km corridor through the city centre.
eli: A stream in the middle of Seoul was covered with concrete and a highway was built on top.
The city took the highway down and opened the stream up again.
Now people walk beside the water in the heart of the city.
