src.name: Encyclopedia of Korean Culture (Academy of Korean Studies), Cheonggyecheon restoration project

asiaoceania.credit: Image: NASA (iss072e757318)

asiaoceania.sum: In 2000, the Chilika Development Authority opened a new mouth between India's Chilika Lake and the sea, and the lagoon and its fisheries recovered (CDA).
eli: Chilika is a huge lagoon in India where river water and seawater mix.
Mud was choking its link to the sea, so fish and the people who catch them were struggling.
Engineers dug a new opening to the sea, and the fish came back.
asiaoceania.credit: Image: Phadke09 via Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

asiaoceania.sum: Coral Gardeners grows corals in nurseries and replants them on reefs in French Polynesia, Fiji and Thailand: 238,250 corals planted so far.
eli: Coral reefs are like busy underwater cities for fish, and many are getting sick from hot water.
Coral Gardeners grow baby corals in underwater nurseries, like a garden.
When the corals are big enough, divers plant them back on the reef so it can grow again.
asiaoceania.credit: Image: NASA (STS093-717-066)

asiaoceania.sum: Researchers capture coral spawn and rear millions of baby corals for damaged reefs; the first Coral IVF corals reproduced on the Great Barrier Reef in 2021.
eli: Once a year, corals let out tiny eggs into the sea at the same time.
Scientists catch them and help millions of baby corals grow in special pools.
Then they put the babies on hurt reefs so the reefs can grow back.

src.name: Great Barrier Reef Foundation, What is Coral IVF?

asiaoceania.alt: A coral releasing a burst of eggs and sperm into the water during spawning in Flower Garden Banks National Marine Sanctuary
asiaoceania.credit: Image: G.P. Schmahl/NOAA (public domain)

asiaoceania.sum: India's EOS-06, the third Oceansat, tracks ocean color, sea-surface temperature and winds; it imaged Cyclone Mandous and an algal bloom on day one.
eli: What is it? An ocean satellite with color, temperature and wind sensors.
Why does it matter? Continuity of ocean color and wind data for fisheries, cyclones and coasts.
asiaoceania.credit: Image: ISRO/NASA/JPL-Caltech (PIA14742)

asiaoceania.sum: Earth Fire Alliance's FireSat satellites are built to spot wildfires as small as 5 by 5 meters from space and get the data to firefighters fast.
eli: Wildfires are much easier to stop while they are still small.
FireSat satellites carry special cameras that can sense heat from space.
They can spot a fire about the size of two parking spaces and help firefighters act fast.

src.name: Earth Fire Alliance, FireSat first light (Sep 16, 2026)

asiaoceania.credit: Image: NASA

asiaoceania.sum: Japan's SHIKISAI satellite checks the health of Earth from space every 2 or 3 days, tracking clouds, aerosols, ocean color, plants, snow and ice (JAXA).
eli: GCOM-C, also called SHIKISAI, is a Japanese satellite that looks at the whole Earth.
It sees clouds, tiny particles in the air, plants, ocean color, snow and ice.
This helps scientists understand climate change.
asiaoceania.credit: Image: NASA (ISS074-E-0046371)

asiaoceania.sum: On 5 July 2026, JAXA's Hayabusa2 passed about 400 m above asteroid Torifune, the closest flyby of any Solar System body so far (JAXA).
eli: Hayabusa2 is a Japanese spacecraft that once brought pieces of an asteroid back to Earth.
In July 2026 it zoomed past another asteroid, Torifune, closer than any spacecraft ever flew past a space rock.
Aiming that well means we could one day hit a dangerous asteroid and push it away.

src.name: JAXA, Hayabusa2 sets a new record for closest flyby

asiaoceania.alt: Asteroid Ryugu, photographed by Hayabusa2 in 2018 before it went on to Torifune
asiaoceania.credit: Image: JAXA Hayabusa2 ONC data, processed by Anonymsiy (CC BY 4.0)

asiaoceania.sum: India's INSAT-3DS watches weather, land and oceans from geostationary orbit and carries a search-and-rescue transponder (ISRO).
eli: INSAT-3DS is an Indian weather satellite that stays over the same place above Earth.
It takes pictures of clouds, rain, fog and fires.
It also passes on distress calls so rescuers can find people in trouble.
asiaoceania.credit: Image: NASA (STS102-357-031)
places: Satish Dhawan Space Centre, Sriharikota, India (launch site)

asiaoceania.sum: New Zealand's Department of Conservation and Ngāi Tahu have rebuilt the kākāpō from just 51 birds in 1995 (NZ DOC).
eli: The kākāpō is a big, green parrot from New Zealand that cannot fly.
By 1995, only 51 were left.
Rangers watched over every nest and helped chicks grow up, and now there are 325.

src.name: NZ Department of Conservation, Kākāpō population reaches new milestone (1 Sept. 2026)

asiaoceania.credit: Image: NZ Department of Conservation via Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 2.0)

asiaoceania.n: Lake Biwa and the Soap Movement
asiaoceania.sum: After a red tide in 1977, Shiga residents switched to soap, and in 1980 the prefecture limited phosphorus to protect Lake Biwa (Shiga Prefecture).
eli: Lake Biwa is the biggest lake in Japan.
Phosphorus from washing detergent fed tiny algae until the water turned red in 1977.
People switched to natural soap, and new rules cut the phosphorus going into the lake.

src.name: Shiga Prefecture, Think about life by seeing Lake Biwa

asiaoceania.alt: Lake Biwa and the Soap Movement
asiaoceania.credit: Image: NASA (ISS007-E-17620)

asiaoceania.sum: Since 1998, the Global Nature Fund's Living Lakes Network has protected and restored lakes and wetlands with 130 member organizations in more than 60 countries.
eli: Living Lakes is a team of groups that look after lakes all over the world.
They clean up trash and help people near lakes earn money without harming nature.
In Mongolia they help protect a lake that is about 2 million years old.

asiaoceania.sum: India's Namami Gange programme has created or rehabilitated 4,263 million litres a day of sewage treatment for the River Ganga (government figures).
eli: The Ganga is a huge, holy river in India.
Too much dirty water from towns was flowing into it.
India is building treatment plants to clean that water before it reaches the river.

src.name: Press Information Bureau (Ministry of Jal Shakti), 19th Empowered Task Force on River Ganga, 2 July 2026

asiaoceania.alt: Contribute to the Clean Ganga Fund
asiaoceania.credit: Image: NASA (ISS070-E-005997)
places: Varanasi, on the River Ganga, India

asiaoceania.sum: With rangers, wildlife corridors and over 450 community anti-poaching units, Nepal nearly tripled its wild tigers in 13 years (NTNC).
eli: Tigers were disappearing from Asia because of hunting and lost forests.
Nepal promised to double its tigers, and protected forests and paths between them.
Local communities helped stop poachers, and now Nepal has about three times as many tigers.

src.name: NTNC, Nepal is the first country to double its tiger population (July 2022)

asiaoceania.credit: Image: Ambish Kazi via Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

asiaoceania.sum: NEWater is high-grade reclaimed water from PUB, Singapore's National Water Agency, made from treated used water in a three-step purification process at 4 plants.
eli: Singapore is a small island without much room to store rain.
So it takes water that has already been used, cleans it with special filters and ultraviolet light, and makes it ultra-clean.
Factories use most of it, and in dry spells some is added to reservoirs.

src.name: PUB, Singapore's National Water Agency, NEWater

asiaoceania.credit: Image: NASA (iss073e0763866)

asiaoceania.sum: The Palau National Marine Sanctuary makes about 80% of Palau's exclusive economic zone a no-take area, with the other 20% kept as a Domestic Fishing Zone.
eli: Palau is a country made of islands in the Pacific Ocean.
It decided that most of its ocean should be a place where nobody fishes.
That gives sea life room to grow back and spill over into the areas where local people fish.

src.name: Palau International Coral Reef Center, PNMS Act enters into full force (Jan. 1, 2020)

asiaoceania.credit: Image: NASA Earth Observatory/Jesse Allen, Landsat 8 data from USGS

asiaoceania.sum: Plastic Bank pays collectors in vulnerable communities to gather ocean-bound plastic, exchanged at local branches for income, food vouchers and school supplies.
eli: What is it? A global bottle-deposit program: collectors in vulnerable communities gather ocean-bound plastic and exchange it at local branches for income, food vouchers, health insurance, and school supplies, all tracked on a blockchain platform.

Why does it matter? Most ocean plastic starts as land-based waste in places with weak waste infrastructure. Making plastic valuable at the source stops it before it enters rivers and the sea, while paying collectors directly.

src.name: Plastic Bank newsletter, June 2026 (all-time data as of June 10, 2026)

asiaoceania.sum: Predator Free 2050 is a nationwide goal to eradicate rats, possums, feral cats and mustelids from Aotearoa New Zealand, led by the Department of Conservation.
eli: New Zealand's birds grew up with no mammals that hunt them.
Then people brought rats, stoats, possums and cats, which eat birds and their eggs.
The country is working to remove those predators everywhere by 2050.
asiaoceania.credit: Image: NASA (iss071e073568)

asiaoceania.sum: Solar-powered Guardian listening devices and SI detect chainsaws in real time; Rainforest Connection reports more than 726,000 hectares of rainforest protected.
eli: Rainforest Connection puts listening boxes high up in trees.
The boxes use the sun for power and a computer that can tell when it hears a chainsaw.
When it hears one, a ranger gets a message on a phone and can go stop the cutting.
asiaoceania.alt: Landsat views of the same patch of Amazon rainforest in Rondônia, Brazil: unbroken forest in 1975 (left) and the fishbone pattern of clearings along roads in 2012 (right)
asiaoceania.credit: Image: NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center/Landsat (public domain)

asiaoceania.sum: River Cleanup and its volunteers have recovered more than 4.39 million kg of waste from rivers worldwide and aim for 1,000 plastic-free rivers by 2050.
eli: River Cleanup is a group that picks up trash in rivers.
More than a million helpers have joined.
Catching trash in rivers stops it from reaching the ocean.
asiaoceania.alt: Volunteers in rafts and kayaks collecting trash from the Trinity River in California
asiaoceania.credit: Image: David Byers, BLM (public domain)

asiaoceania.n: Saiga Recovery on the Kazakh Steppe (Altyn Dala)
asiaoceania.sum: The Altyn Dala Conservation Initiative, led by ACBK, is restoring Kazakhstan's steppe, with the saiga antelope as its flagship (Altyn Dala).
eli: The saiga is an antelope with a big, bendy nose that lives on the grassy steppe.
Not long ago, there were very few left in Kazakhstan.
Kazakhstan and its partners protected the steppe, and now there are millions again.

src.name: Altyn Dala Conservation Initiative, 2024 saiga aerial census results

asiaoceania.alt: Saiga Recovery on the Kazakh Steppe (Altyn Dala)
asiaoceania.credit: Image: Yakov Fedorov via Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)
places: The Kazakh steppe, Altyn Dala landscape, Kazakhstan

asiaoceania.sum: Seabin's floating bins have captured 33.2 million items in Sydney Harbour since 2020, including 19.0 million microplastics (company figures).
eli: What is it? Seabins: floating trash skimmers in marinas and ports, plus a live data dashboard.
Why does it matter? Microplastics and plastic pollution threaten our health and the environment.
How does it help people? Seabin monitors as well as removes, giving cities live data on plastic pollution, which it says threatens our health (company description).
asiaoceania.credit: Image: NASA/GSFC/METI/ERSDAC/JAROS and U.S./Japan ASTER Science Team (PIA03498)

asiaoceania.sum: SeaTrees connects people with local partners restoring mangroves, coral reefs, kelp forests and seagrass meadows around the world (SeaTrees).
eli: "Seatrees" are ocean plants like mangroves , kelp and seagrass .
SeaTrees helps people plant and protect them with help from local teams.
These plants give fish a home and protect beaches from big storms.
asiaoceania.alt: A restoration worker places repotted mangrove seedlings in a marshy channel at Kennedy Space Center
asiaoceania.credit: Image: NASA/Glenn Benson (KSC-20230412-PH-GEB01_0152)

asiaoceania.sum: Sungai Watch stops plastic in Indonesian rivers with trash barriers, daily collection and sorting, plus upcycling, working in Bali and Java since 2020.
eli: What is it? Custom trash barriers in rivers, then daily collection, sorting into material categories, and upcycling through Sungai Design. Sungai means river in Indonesian.
Why does it matter? Indonesia’s rivers carry a large share of plastic toward the sea. Barriers plus paid local crews stop it before it leaves the island.

asiaoceania.sum: Tanager-1, built by Planet with a NASA JPL-designed spectrometer for the nonprofit Carbon Mapper, pinpoints methane and CO2 plumes from single sources.
eli: What is it? A satellite that pinpoints methane and carbon dioxide plumes from individual sources.
Why does it matter? Finding single leaks lets operators and regulators fix them fast.

src.name: NASA, First greenhouse gas plumes detected

asiaoceania.credit: Image: Carbon Mapper/Planet Labs PBC (PIA26416)

asiaoceania.sum: Mobula cleanup boats catch plastic close to where it starts, and in Malaysia one boat turned 135,000 pieces of debris into community walkways (The SeaCleaners).
eli: The SeaCleaners use special boats called Mobulas to scoop plastic out of the water.
They work with local people so the cleanup keeps going after they leave.
Some of the plastic is recycled into useful things, like walkways.
asiaoceania.credit: Image: NASA (STS066-154-157)

asiaoceania.n: Tonle Sap: The Lake That Reverses a River
asiaoceania.sum: Tonle Sap, the largest freshwater lake in Southeast Asia, is a UNESCO biosphere reserve whose flooded forests shelter villages and fish (UNESCO).
eli: Tonle Sap is a giant lake in Cambodia joined to the Mekong River.
In the rainy season the river gets so full that water flows backwards into the lake.
The lake swells up, flooding forests where fish grow, and many families live in floating villages.

src.name: UNESCO Man and the Biosphere Programme, Tonle Sap

asiaoceania.alt: Tonle Sap: The Lake That Reverses a River
asiaoceania.credit: Image: Christophe95 via Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

asiaoceania.sum: Tubbataha, a no-take marine park of 96,828 hectares in the Philippines, protects pristine coral atolls and the sea life that seeds the Sulu Sea (UNESCO).
eli: Tubbataha is a group of coral reefs far out in the sea in the Philippines.
Nobody is allowed to fish there, so the fish can grow big and have lots of babies.
Baby fish drift out from the reef and help fill fishing grounds around it.

src.name: IUCN World Heritage Outlook, Tubbataha Reefs Natural Park

asiaoceania.credit: Image: Ron Van Oers/UNESCO via Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 3.0 IGO)
places: Tubbataha Reefs Natural Park, Sulu Sea, Philippines

asiaoceania.sum: Waterkeeper Alliance unites hundreds of local Waterkeeper groups that patrol and protect more than 6 million square miles of rivers, lakes and coastlines.
eli: A Waterkeeper is a person or group who watches over a river, lake or coast.
They check the water and stop people from polluting it.
It all started with fishermen who saved the Hudson River in New York.

orbit.sum: JAXA's DAICHI-4 radar sees through clouds over a 200 km swath, continuing the radar record used for deforestation alerts.
eli: What is it? A radar satellite with the PALSAR-3 L-band synthetic aperture radar and a ship-tracking receiver.
Why does it matter? Forests cover 30% of the world's land, and deforestation is strongly linked to rising greenhouse gases .
orbit.alt: ALOS-4 "DAICHI-4": JAXA's 1/50 scale model of the satellite, with its PALSAR-3 radar antenna and solar arrays, at Tsukuba Space Center
orbit.credit: Image: Syced, via Wikimedia Commons (CC0)

orbit.sum: A satellite system that tracks wildlife and ocean instruments from tiny transmitters, following more than 8,000 animals every month for conservation science.
eli: Scientists put a tiny radio tag on a turtle, bird or whale.
Satellites pick up the tag's signal and work out where the animal is.
Knowing where animals travel helps people protect them.

src.name: NOAA OSPO, Argos Data Collection System

orbit.alt: An adult false killer whale surfacing off Guam, photographed by NOAA scientists before a satellite tag was attached
orbit.credit: Image: Adam U / NOAA/NMFS/Pacific Islands Fisheries Science Center (public domain)

orbit.n: ATLAS Asteroid Terrestrial-impact Last Alert System
orbit.sum: Four robotic telescopes, two in Hawaiʻi, search the entire dark sky every 24 hours for asteroids that could hit Earth, so people can be warned.
eli: ATLAS is four robot telescopes that scan the night sky.
They look for space rocks that come close to Earth.
An early warning gives people time to get ready or move away.

src.name: NASA, ATLAS now capable of full-sky search

orbit.alt: The island of Hawaiʻi, home of Mauna Loa, seen from the International Space Station

orbit.sum: ESA's Biomass satellite, launched April 29, 2025, carries the first P-band radar in space, seeing through forest canopies to measure the carbon stored in trees.
eli: What is it? The first P-band synthetic aperture radar in space.
Why does it matter? To measure the woody biomass where forests store carbon, and track deforestation and regrowth.
orbit.alt: Biomass (ESA) – Earth Observation

orbit.sum: A NASA-funded survey in Arizona that has discovered more near-Earth objects than any other: 17,930 near-Earth asteroids since 1995.
eli: Catalina is a team in Arizona that hunts for space rocks every clear night.
They have found more near-Earth asteroids than anyone else.
They even spotted a small one hours before it burned up over Africa.
orbit.alt: Discovery images of asteroid 2018 LA, a faint moving dot, taken hours before it entered Earth's atmosphere

orbit.sum: CHIME will image Earth in more than 200 colours of light to support sustainable farming, food security and biodiversity (ESA).
eli: CHIME will be two satellites that see far more colours than our eyes can.
Those colours show how healthy crops and soils are.
Farmers and scientists can use this to grow food and protect nature.
orbit.alt: Patchwork of farm fields in Montana's Golden Triangle, seen by Landsat
orbit.credit: Image: NASA Earth Observatory/Lauren Dauphin, Landsat data from USGS (public domain)

orbit.sum: Three spacecraft will wait in space for a fresh comet and fly past it together to make a 3D map; launch is planned for late 2028 or early 2029 (ESA).
eli: Some comets come from very far away and have never been near the Sun before.
Comet Interceptor will wait in space until scientists find one.
Then three spacecraft fly past it together to make a 3D picture.
orbit.alt: Comet Interceptor (ESA / JAXA)

orbit.sum: Europe's air monitoring service forecasts air pollution, smoke and dust worldwide twice a day for more than 23,500 users, free and open.
eli: CAMS checks the air all over the world, from smoke to dust to pollution.
It uses satellites and computer models to forecast dirty air days ahead.
People can plan to stay safe on bad air days.

src.name: Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service, About us

orbit.alt: Smoke from fires on Sumatra blowing toward Malaysia and Singapore, seen by NASA's Aqua satellite

orbit.n: Copernicus CO2M Carbon Dioxide Monitoring (ESA / EU)
orbit.sum: A planned trio of satellites that will measure the carbon dioxide and methane people release, so countries can check whether their emission cuts are working.
eli: Some gases, like carbon dioxide , trap heat and warm our planet.
CO2M will be three satellites that measure how much of these gases people release.
That helps countries see if their plans to cut pollution are working.

src.name: ESA, Europe’s carbon dioxide monitoring mission elevated to the power of three

orbit.alt: Artist's view of a Copernicus CO2M satellite in orbit measuring carbon dioxide from human activity
orbit.credit: Image: ESA/Mlabspace (CC BY-SA 3.0 IGO)

orbit.n: Copernicus Emergency Management Service: On-Demand Mapping
orbit.sum: The European Union's emergency mapping service turns satellite images into maps for disaster teams, 24/7 since 2012, with more than 1,000 activations.
eli: When a disaster happens, helpers need to know which roads and houses are damaged.
Copernicus EMS uses satellite pictures to draw those maps quickly.
It works day and night and has helped more than 120 countries.
orbit.alt: Smoke from wildfires burning across central Canada, photographed from the International Space Station

orbit.sum: Free, open ocean data and forecasts for the whole planet. In 2025 users downloaded almost 15,000 terabytes of ocean data from Copernicus Marine.
eli: Copernicus Marine is like a weather service for the ocean.
It shows ocean temperature, currents, sea ice and tiny plant life.
Sailors, scientists and fishers use it for free.
orbit.alt: Swirls of a phytoplankton bloom in the deep blue central North Atlantic Ocean, seen by satellite
orbit.credit: Image: NASA/GSFC/Jeff Schmaltz/MODIS Land Rapid Response Team

orbit.sum: Sentinel-1 radar sees through clouds, day and night, to map floods, earthquakes and ice; Sentinel-1C and 1D joined in 2024 and 2025.
eli: What is it? Radar satellites imaging Earth through cloud and darkness.
Why does it matter? Continuous radar imagery for disaster response, ice, land and ocean monitoring.
orbit.alt: Copernicus Sentinel-1 (ESA)

orbit.sum: Sentinel-2C joined the Copernicus fleet in September 2024, imaging land and coasts in 13 bands so forests and crops are checked every five days.
eli: What is it? A satellite with a multispectral imager covering 13 spectral bands, with a 290 km swath and detail down to 10 m.
Why does it matter? To monitor agriculture, forests, land-use change, coastal and inland waters, and disasters.
How does it help people? Farmers use Sentinel-2 data to monitor crop health, predict yields and practice precision farming, and responders use it to map floods, wildfires and eruptions.
orbit.alt: Lighthouse Reef and the Great Blue Hole off Belize in one of the first images from Copernicus Sentinel-2C
orbit.credit: Image: contains modified Copernicus Sentinel data (2024), processed by ESA (CC BY-SA 3.0 IGO)

orbit.sum: The Copernicus Sentinel-3 satellites measure Earth's oceans, land, ice and atmosphere, and a third satellite, Sentinel-3C, launched on September 15, 2026 (ESA).
eli: Sentinel-3 satellites check the oceans, land and ice all the time.
They measure how warm the sea is, how high it is, and even spot fires.
Weather and ocean forecasters use this to keep people safe.
orbit.alt: Sunset over Antarctica captured by the Copernicus Sentinel-3B satellite
orbit.credit: Image: contains modified Copernicus Sentinel data (2018), processed by EUMETSAT (CC BY-SA 3.0 IGO)

orbit.sum: From geostationary orbit on MTG-S1, Sentinel-4 measures air pollution such as nitrogen dioxide and ozone over Europe and North Africa every hour (ESA).
eli: Sentinel-4 is a space tool that watches the air over Europe.
It stays above the same spot and checks the air every hour.
This helps warn people when the air is dirty.
orbit.alt: Europe and North Africa seen by Copernicus Sentinel-4 from geostationary orbit
orbit.credit: Image: contains modified Copernicus Sentinel data (2025), processed by ESA (CC BY-SA 3.0 IGO)

orbit.sum: Copernicus Sentinel-5P maps the gases in the air we breathe, covering the whole planet every day with its Tropomi instrument (ESA).
eli: Sentinel-5P is a satellite that sniffs the air from space.
Every day it checks the whole planet for gases that make air dirty.
This helps keep people healthy and track gases that warm Earth.
orbit.alt: World map of average nitrogen dioxide pollution in 2014 measured from space by the Ozone Monitoring Instrument on NASA's Aura satellite, brightest over big cities and industrial areas
orbit.credit: Image: NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center (public domain)

orbit.sum: Sentinel-6B, launched November 17, 2025, continues the precise record of global sea level that began in the early 1990s.
eli: What is it? A radar altimetry satellite that measures the height of the sea surface.
Why does it matter? An unbroken sea-level record helps coastal cities plan for rising water.
orbit.alt: Copernicus Sentinel-6B (ESA / NASA)

orbit.sum: NOAA's Coral Reef Watch uses satellites to warn of the ocean heat that bleaches corals, with daily monitoring of 95% of the world's coral reefs.
eli: Corals are tiny animals that build reefs, and too much heat makes them turn white.
NOAA satellites check the ocean's temperature every day.
Reef managers use the warnings to protect corals before it is too late.

src.name: NOAA Coral Reef Watch, Satellite Bleaching Alert emails

orbit.alt: Reefs of the Great Barrier Reef off the coast of Queensland, Australia, seen from the International Space Station

orbit.sum: Digital Earth Africa turns satellite data into free and open maps of water, farmland and coasts for the whole African continent (Digital Earth Africa).
eli: Satellites take pictures of Africa all the time, but the raw data is hard to use.
Digital Earth Africa cleans it up and turns it into ready-made maps.
Anyone can use them for free to track water, crops and coastlines.
orbit.alt: Digital Earth Africa – Earth Observation

orbit.sum: NASA's EPIC camera rides on NOAA's DSCOVR spacecraft at the L1 point, photographing the entire sunlit face of Earth several times a day, with an archive...
eli: What is it? A camera photographing the entire sunlit face of Earth several times a day.
Why does it matter? Daily whole-Earth views, including ozone measurements, track our changing planet.
orbit.alt: DSCOVR / EPIC (NASA–NOAA)

orbit.sum: ESA–JAXA EarthCARE carries the first space cloud radar that can measure how cloud particles move up and down, sharpening forecasts of how clouds affect climate.
eli: What is it? A satellite with four instruments, including JAXA's Doppler Cloud Profiling Radar .
Why does it matter? Knowing whether clouds warm or cool the planet sharpens climate forecasts.
orbit.alt: EarthCARE (ESA–JAXA) – Earth Observation

orbit.sum: NASA's EMIT instrument on the International Space Station maps the minerals in desert dust and has spotted methane super-emitters from space (NASA JPL).
eli: EMIT is a special camera on the International Space Station.
It splits sunlight into many colors to tell what the ground is made of.
It also spotted big leaks of methane , a gas that heats the planet, so they can be fixed.
orbit.alt: EMIT (NASA) – Earth Observation

orbit.sum: India's EOS-06, the third Oceansat, tracks ocean color, sea-surface temperature and winds; it imaged Cyclone Mandous and an algal bloom on day one.
eli: What is it? An ocean satellite with color, temperature and wind sensors.
Why does it matter? Continuity of ocean color and wind data for fisheries, cyclones and coasts.
orbit.alt: EOS-06 / Oceansat-3 (ISRO)

orbit.sum: Europe's wildfire system forecasts fire danger and maps burnt areas from satellites. In 2024 it mapped wildfires in 42 countries.
eli: EFFIS warns when the weather makes forest fires likely.
After a fire, satellites show exactly how much land burned.
Countries use this to fight fires and plan how forests recover.
orbit.alt: Smoke from wildfires near the southern coast of Portugal, photographed from the International Space Station

orbit.sum: Earth Fire Alliance's FireSat satellites are built to spot wildfires as small as 5 by 5 meters from space and get the data to firefighters fast.
eli: Wildfires are much easier to stop while they are still small.
FireSat satellites carry special cameras that can sense heat from space.
They can spot a fire about the size of two parking spaces and help firefighters act fast.

src.name: Earth Fire Alliance, FireSat first light (Sep 16, 2026)

orbit.alt: FireSat (Earth Fire Alliance)

orbit.n: FIRMS Fire Information for Resource Management System (NASA)
orbit.sum: NASA's FIRMS delivers satellite fire detections within 3 hours anywhere on Earth, and in real time for the US and Canada. Free for firefighters and everyone.
eli: Satellites can feel the heat of a fire from space.
FIRMS puts those hot spots on a free map within a few hours.
Firefighters and farmers can even get an email when a fire starts nearby.
orbit.alt: Wildfires burning across Canada's central provinces, with smoke drifting south, seen from the International Space Station

orbit.sum: Launched together on September 15, 2026, ESA's FLEX maps the faint glow of photosynthesis while Sentinel-3C watches oceans and land.
eli: What is it? FLEX maps plant fluorescence; Sentinel-3C measures ocean and land.
Why does it matter? To understand plant health, photosynthesis and the carbon cycle.
orbit.alt: A strip of OCO-3 satellite measurements showing the faint fluorescence glow plants give off during photosynthesis, darker green where plants are more active, across the Caucasus region

orbit.sum: ESA's FORUM will measure Earth's outgoing far-infrared radiation, never measured from space before, filling a missing piece of the climate jigsaw (ESA).
eli: Earth gives off heat into space as invisible infrared light.
Part of that light, called far-infrared, has never been measured from space.
FORUM will measure it, helping scientists understand how Earth keeps its heat balance.
orbit.alt: NOAA world map of the infrared (longwave) energy Earth sends back out to space
orbit.credit: Image: NOAA NESDIS (public domain)

orbit.sum: Europe's Galileo is the world's most precise satellite navigation system, serving over five billion smartphone users and helping rescues (ESA).
eli: Galileo is a group of satellites that tells your phone exactly where it is.
Each satellite has very accurate atomic clocks.
Galileo satellites can also hear emergency beacons and pass the alert to rescuers.

src.name: ESA, Two new Galileo satellites enter service

orbit.alt: A Galileo navigation satellite inside ESA's acoustic test chamber in the Netherlands
orbit.credit: Image: ESA-Anneke Le Floc'h (CC BY-SA 3.0 IGO)

orbit.sum: Japan's SHIKISAI satellite checks the health of Earth from space every 2 or 3 days, tracking clouds, aerosols, ocean color, plants, snow and ice (JAXA).
eli: GCOM-C, also called SHIKISAI, is a Japanese satellite that looks at the whole Earth.
It sees clouds, tiny particles in the air, plants, ocean color, snow and ice.
This helps scientists understand climate change.
orbit.alt: GCOM-C "SHIKISAI" (JAXA)

orbit.sum: GEDI fires lasers from the International Space Station to measure the height and 3D shape of Earth's forests (University of Maryland).
eli: GEDI is a laser tool on the International Space Station.
It shines light down on forests and times how long it takes to bounce back.
That tells scientists how tall trees are and how much carbon forests hold.

src.name: University of Maryland, GEDI mission overview

orbit.alt: The GEDI forest-mapping laser instrument mounted outside Japan's Kibo module on the International Space Station

orbit.sum: NOAA's next generation of geostationary weather satellites, planned from 2032, will improve warnings of severe weather and hazards (NOAA).
eli: GeoXO will be new weather satellites that stay over the same spot above Earth.
They will watch storms, wildfires, smoke and floods as they happen.
This helps forecasters warn people sooner.
orbit.alt: Visualization of the planned GeoXO East satellite above Earth with the scanning pattern of its ocean color instrument
orbit.credit: Image: NASA's Scientific Visualization Studio (public domain)

orbit.sum: JAXA's IBUKI GW tracks carbon dioxide, methane and nitrogen dioxide while also measuring the water cycle. Launched June 29, 2025 from Tanegashima Space Center.
eli: What is it? A satellite carrying TANSO-3 for greenhouse gases and AMSR3 for the water cycle.
Why does it matter? Countries need independent, consistent measurements of emissions to check climate pledges.
orbit.alt: NASA satellite map of carbon dioxide around the world from space, the greenhouse gas Japan's IBUKI GW satellite also measures

orbit.sum: Twin US-German satellites weigh Earth's water by measuring gravity, tracking groundwater, ice and sea level since 2018. Active.
eli: What is it? Twin satellites measuring Earth's changing gravity field.
Why does it matter? To track water in aquifers, ice and oceans, for drought and water planning.
orbit.alt: GRACE-FO (NASA / Germany)

orbit.sum: JAXA's Global Satellite Mapping of Precipitation maps rain around the world every hour, used by 18,673 registered users in 163 countries and regions.
eli: GSMaP is a map that shows where it is raining all over the world.
It mixes data from many satellites and updates every hour.
Scientists use it to watch rain as it falls and to study climate.

src.name: JAXA EORC, GSMaP talk at IPWG-12 (July 2026)

orbit.alt: The GPM Microwave Imager installed on the GPM Core Observatory in a NASA Goddard cleanroom

orbit.sum: On 5 July 2026, JAXA's Hayabusa2 passed about 400 m above asteroid Torifune, the closest flyby of any Solar System body so far (JAXA).
eli: Hayabusa2 is a Japanese spacecraft that once brought pieces of an asteroid back to Earth.
In July 2026 it zoomed past another asteroid, Torifune, closer than any spacecraft ever flew past a space rock.
Aiming that well means we could one day hit a dangerous asteroid and push it away.

src.name: JAXA, Hayabusa2 sets a new record for closest flyby

orbit.alt: Asteroid Ryugu, photographed by Hayabusa2 in 2018 before it went on to Torifune
orbit.credit: Image: JAXA Hayabusa2 ONC data, processed by Anonymsiy (CC BY 4.0)

orbit.sum: ESA's Hera arrives at the asteroid Dimorphos in November 2026 to measure what NASA's DART impact did, turning deflection into a repeatable defense.
eli: What is it? A small, van-sized deep-space spacecraft that will perform a close-up "crash scene investigation" of Dimorphos, measuring its mass, its shifted orbit and DART's impact crater. Juventas will make the first radar sounding inside an asteroid .
Why does it matter? To turn DART's one-off hit into a well-understood, repeatable technique for defending Earth from hazardous asteroids, by measuring how much push the impact really delivered.
orbit.alt: Hera: Investigating the Asteroid DART Moved
orbit.credit: Image: ESA – Science Office (CC BY-SA 3.0 IGO, resized)

orbit.sum: ESA's first Scout mission uses reflected navigation-satellite signals to measure soil moisture, wetlands and frozen ground (ESA).
eli: Navigation satellites send signals that bounce off the ground.
HydroGNSS catches those echoes to tell how wet the soil is.
That helps farmers, flood planners and scientists watch Earth's water.
orbit.alt: NASA SMAP world map of surface soil moisture, August 25-27, 2015

orbit.sum: India's INSAT-3DS watches weather, land and oceans from geostationary orbit and carries a search-and-rescue transponder (ISRO).
eli: INSAT-3DS is an Indian weather satellite that stays over the same place above Earth.
It takes pictures of clouds, rain, fog and fires.
It also passes on distress calls so rescuers can find people in trouble.
orbit.alt: INSAT-3DS Weather Satellite (ISRO)

orbit.n: International Charter: Space and Major Disasters
orbit.sum: When disaster strikes, 17 space agencies and satellite operators pool their satellites and give free images to rescue teams. Activated 1,000 times.
eli: When a big flood or earthquake happens, rescuers need a map fast.
Space agencies around the world agree to point their satellites at the disaster.
They give the pictures away for free, so helpers know where people need them.
orbit.alt: Muddy floodwater from the Missouri River covering fields near Hamburg, Iowa, seen from orbit

orbit.sum: NOAA's polar weather satellites circle Earth 14 times a day. Polar-orbiting satellites supply about 85% of the data used by weather prediction models.
eli: JPSS satellites fly over the North and South Poles, around and around.
They scan the whole Earth twice a day for temperature, clouds and rain.
Forecasters use the data to warn people before hurricanes and blizzards.

src.name: NOAA NESDIS, Joint Polar Satellite System

orbit.alt: NOAA's JPSS-2 weather satellite on its Atlas V rocket at the launch pad in California

orbit.sum: Landsat 9 continues a 50-year record of Earth’s land, collecting 740 scenes a day and, with Landsat 8, seeing each place every 8 days.
eli: What is it? The latest Landsat satellite, collecting 740 scenes of Earth each day, almost double its minimum requirement.
Why does it matter? The longest continuous satellite record of Earth’s land surface shows how forests, water and farms change.

How does it help people? Landsat supports water management in drought-prone regions where farms, industry and communities compete for water, and its free data added an estimated $25.6 billion to the U.S. economy in 2023.
orbit.alt: Landsat 9 (NASA / USGS) – Earth Observation

orbit.sum: Libera will measure how much energy leaves Earth each day, keeping a climate record that began in 2000 going strong (NOAA).
eli: Sunlight brings energy to Earth, and Earth sends some back to space.
Libera will measure how much energy leaves our planet each day.
If more comes in than goes out, Earth warms, so this helps track climate.
orbit.alt: Globe map of sunlight reflected back to space over Africa and Europe, measured by NASA's CERES instrument, the Earth energy record that Libera continues
orbit.credit: Image: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center (public domain)

orbit.sum: NASA's Lucy is touring asteroids; after Dinkinesh and Donaldjohanson, it reaches its first Trojan asteroid, Eurybates, on 11 August 2027 (NASA).
eli: Lucy is a NASA spacecraft that visits many asteroids , one after another.
Some asteroids travel with Jupiter around the Sun. They are very old.
Studying them is like reading fossils of how the planets were made.
orbit.alt: Lucy (NASA) – Planetary Defense

orbit.sum: Three weather satellites now watch Europe and Africa from 36,000 km up, with new images every 2.5 minutes and a camera that catches lightning day and night.
eli: Meteosat Third Generation is a team of weather satellites that watch Europe and Africa.
One camera takes a new picture of the weather every 2.5 minutes.
Another camera spots lightning, which helps warn people about dangerous storms.

src.name: ESA, MTG-I2 completes Europe's latest weather trio

orbit.alt: Meteosat Third Generation (ESA / EUMETSAT)

orbit.sum: The UN's satellite methane alert system has sent more than 3,500 alerts about major leaks in 33 countries, and responses rose from 1% to 12% in a year.
eli: Methane is a gas that heats the planet, and big leaks can be seen from space.
The United Nations watches satellite data and tells countries and companies about leaks.
When they fix a leak, the air gets cleaner and the planet heats up less.

src.name: UNEP IMEO, Methane Alert and Response System

orbit.alt: A cluster of methane plumes detected from orbit in southern Uzbekistan, shown in color over a satellite map

orbit.sum: Launched August 2025 on Ariane 6, MetOp-SG-A1 carries Sentinel-5, which delivers daily global data on air pollutants, ozone and climate gases.
eli: What is it? The first MetOp Second Generation weather satellite, carrying the Copernicus Sentinel-5 air-quality instrument.
Why does it matter? To track air pollution, ozone and climate gases, and to sharpen weather forecasts.

How does it help people? Daily air-pollution data help authorities monitor pollution and make decisions, and better weather data matter: EUMETSAT notes extreme weather has cost Europe tens of thousands of lives over the past 40 years.

src.name: ESA, First MetOp-SG satellite and Sentinel-5A launched

orbit.alt: Artist's view of the MetOp-SG A-type and B-type weather satellites in orbit above Earth
orbit.credit: Image: ESA/ATG medialab (CC BY-SA 3.0 IGO)

orbit.sum: Europe's asteroid watch centre computes orbits and impact risks every day and keeps a public list of every asteroid with a non-zero chance of hitting Earth.
eli: Some asteroids pass near Earth, and scientists need to know where they will go.
ESA's centre in Italy collects telescope data and works out their paths.
If an asteroid ever looks dangerous, they warn emergency teams.
orbit.alt: A sequence of radar images of the binary asteroid 2011 UL21 and its small moon

orbit.sum: NASA NEO Surveyor is the first space telescope built to find hazardous asteroids, including dark ones hidden in the Sun's glare. Launch NET September 2027.
eli: What is it? The first space telescope specifically designed to detect asteroids and comets that may be potential hazards to Earth: a single telescope about 50 cm (almost 20 inches) across, seeing in two heat-sensing infrared wavelengths.

Why does it matter? We can only do something about a hazardous asteroid if we find it first. Dark asteroids reflect little visible light but glow in the infrared as sunlight heats them, so an infrared telescope finds what others miss.
orbit.alt: NEO Surveyor: NASA's Asteroid Hunter

orbit.sum: Canada's NEOSSat circles Earth every 100 minutes, scanning near the Sun for asteroids and comets and tracking satellites and debris (CSA).
eli: Some space rocks, called asteroids, pass close to Earth.
NEOSSat is a small Canadian telescope in space that looks for them, even near the Sun.
It also watches satellites and space junk to help avoid crashes in orbit .
orbit.alt: NEOSSat Asteroid and Debris Telescope (Canada)

orbit.sum: NISAR, a NASA and ISRO radar satellite launched from India on July 30, 2025, scans nearly all of Earth's land and ice twice every 12 days, even through clouds.
eli: What is it? A radar satellite carrying NASA's L-band and ISRO's S-band radars.
Why does it matter? Detecting ground and ice motion of about a centimeter helps with earthquakes, landslides, sinking ground, glaciers and crops.
orbit.alt: NISAR (NASA–ISRO) – Earth Observation

orbit.sum: NASA's OCO-2 satellite has measured carbon dioxide around the planet since 2014, showing where carbon is released and where forests and oceans absorb it.
eli: OCO-2 is a satellite that measures carbon dioxide in the air.
It shows where the gas comes from and where plants and oceans soak it up.
It can even see plants glow faintly, which shows how healthy they are.

src.name: NASA, NASA and Caltech partner on two Earth science missions (Aug 24, 2026)

orbit.alt: OCO-2 Orbiting Carbon Observatory (NASA)

orbit.sum: Free satellite data on how much water crops and land use, now for all 48 contiguous states, with more than 13,000 registered users.
eli: Plants drink water and breathe it out into the air.
OpenET uses satellites to measure how much water every field uses.
Farmers can then water only what crops need and save water.
orbit.alt: Red circles of irrigated crops near Garden City, Kansas, in a false-color Landsat 7: Circular crop fields around Garden City, Kansas, seen by Landsat

orbit.sum: On April 13, 2029, asteroid Apophis passes about 20,000 miles from Earth. NASA's OSIRIS-APEX meets it in June 2029 to see how that close pass changes it.
eli: What is it? An asteroid rendezvous mission studying how a close pass of Earth affects a stony asteroid.
Why does it matter? To learn how asteroids respond to gravity and what they are made of, knowledge that informs planetary defense.
orbit.alt: OSIRIS-APEX and Apophis 2029 (NASA)

orbit.sum: NASA's PACE reads the color of the ocean to track phytoplankton, the base of the marine food web, plus aerosols and clouds.
eli: What is it? A satellite whose hyperspectral Ocean Color Instrument measures light from ultraviolet to near-infrared.
Why does it matter? Phytoplankton feed ocean life and help move carbon; tracking them shows how the ocean and climate are changing.
orbit.alt: PACE (NASA) – Earth Observation

orbit.sum: Two telescopes on Haleakalā, Maui, that in 2021 found nearly as many near-Earth objects as the rest of the world's observatories combined.
eli: Pan-STARRS is two big telescopes on a mountain in Maui.
Their giant cameras photograph the sky to find moving space rocks.
Finding them early keeps Earth safe.

src.name: University of Hawaiʻi, Pan-STARRS search for Near-Earth Objects

orbit.alt: Comet C/2025 R3 (PANSTARRS) and its faint tail above Earth's glowing horizon, photographed from the International Space Station

orbit.sum: Three Canadian radar satellites watch Canada's land, coasts and Arctic day and night, through cloud and smoke, with about 250,000 images a year.
eli: RCM is three satellites that use radar , like a bat uses sound.
Radar works in the dark and sees through clouds and smoke.
It helps ships find safe paths through ice and helps after floods.

src.name: Canadian Space Agency, RADARSAT Constellation Mission FAQ

orbit.alt: Swirls of sea ice tracing ocean currents along the coast of Labrador in eastern Canada, photographed from the International Space Station

orbit.sum: ESA and JAXA's Ramses must launch by spring 2028 to meet Apophis before its 2029 Earth pass. Its €81.2 million build contract was signed in February 2026.
eli: What is it? A spacecraft with two CubeSats that will study Apophis before, during and after its Earth pass.
Why does it matter? To understand asteroids ' physical properties and behaviour and strengthen planetary defense.
orbit.alt: Ramses (ESA / JAXA) – Planetary Defense

orbit.sum: NOAA's SARSAT satellites relay distress beacon signals to rescuers; the international system has supported more than 50,000 rescues worldwide since 1982 (NOAA).
eli: Boats, planes and hikers can carry a small emergency beacon.
If they are in trouble, the beacon sends a signal that satellites hear.
The satellites tell rescuers where to go, and that has saved thousands of people.
orbit.alt: Personal locator beacons that send distress signals to COSPAS-SARSAT satellites

orbit.sum: SMAP maps the water in Earth's soil from space, helping improve predictions of weather, floods and droughts (NASA).
eli: SMAP is a satellite that measures how wet or dry the ground is.
It can also tell if the soil is frozen or thawed.
This helps farmers and scientists get ready for floods and droughts.
orbit.alt: Artist's rendering of NASA's SMAP satellite scanning a wide strip of Earth's surface

orbit.sum: SWOT measures more than 95% of Earth's lakes larger than 15 acres and rivers wider than 330 feet, the first global survey of fresh water.
eli: What is it? A radar interferometer satellite that measures the height of water on land and at sea.
Why does it matter? Fresh water is unevenly measured on the ground; SWOT gives every country the same view of its rivers and lakes.
orbit.alt: SWOT (NASA–CNES) – Earth Observation

orbit.sum: Tanager-1, built by Planet with a NASA JPL-designed spectrometer for the nonprofit Carbon Mapper, pinpoints methane and CO2 plumes from single sources.
eli: What is it? A satellite that pinpoints methane and carbon dioxide plumes from individual sources.
Why does it matter? Finding single leaks lets operators and regulators fix them fast.

src.name: NASA, First greenhouse gas plumes detected

orbit.alt: Tanager-1 (Carbon Mapper / Planet)

orbit.sum: From geostationary orbit, NASA's TEMPO measures air pollution over North America every daylight hour, a first from space (NASA).
eli: TEMPO is a space tool that checks how dirty the air is.
It stays above the same spot on Earth and looks at North America every hour while the sun is up.
This helps warn people on bad air days so they can stay safe.
orbit.alt: NASA TEMPO map of nitrogen dioxide air pollution over North America, highest over big cities
orbit.credit: Image: NASA's Scientific Visualization Studio (public domain)

orbit.sum: How the James Webb Space Telescope tracked asteroid 2024 YR4 in February 2026 and ruled out a 2032 Moon impact, two years before ground telescopes could.
eli: What is it? Asteroid 2024 YR4, about 60 meters across, was briefly the most dangerous asteroid found in 20 years. Earth impact was soon ruled out, but a roughly 4% chance of hitting the Moon on December 22, 2032 remained (NASA's last estimate was 4.3%).
Why does it matter? A lunar impact of this scale could affect satellites and future astronauts around the Moon. Knowing years early removes that worry, and proves a technique we can reuse.

src.name: ESA, 2024 YR4 will not impact the Moon

orbit.alt: Webb and Asteroid 2024 YR4: The Moon Is Safe

world.sum: Close to 4,000 robotic floats dive through the ocean and send back temperature and salinity data, free to everyone. The 3 millionth profile came in 2024.
eli: Argo floats are robots that sink deep into the ocean and come back up.
On the way they measure how warm and how salty the water is.
They send the numbers to a satellite, and anyone can use them for free.
world.alt: A Deep SOLO ocean float being lowered into the sea from a research ship

world.sum: Free global river flood forecasts up to 30 days ahead, plus 4-month outlooks, from the Copernicus Emergency Management Service.
eli: GloFAS predicts when rivers might flood, up to a month ahead.
It uses weather forecasts and computer models of rivers.
Early warnings give families time to move to safety.

src.name: CEMS Floods, Monitoring and reporting floods worldwide (March 2024)

world.alt: False-color satellite image of the swollen Kabul River flooding the city of Kheshgi in northwest Pakistan

world.sum: Since 1986, more than 19 million volunteers have collected more than 400 million pounds of trash from beaches and waterways (Ocean Conservancy).
eli: Every year, people around the world clean trash off beaches and rivers on the same day.
They also write down what they find.
That list helps find ways to stop trash from reaching the ocean.
world.alt: Two volunteers picking up trash on Second Beach in Olympic Coast National Marine Sanctuary during the International Coastal Cleanup
world.credit: Image: Karlyn Langjahr/NOAA (public domain)

world.sum: Kelp can grow up to 18 inches a day, building underwater forests that feed and shelter thousands of species. Nature, studied and protected by NOAA and partners.
eli: What is it? Underwater forests of giant algae.
Why does it matter? They feed and shelter thousands of species.

world.sum: Saving Planets' own lake solution: recover plastic from freshwater lakes by skimming, shoreline collection and divers, before it travels downstream to the sea.
eli: What is it? Pulling plastic and litter out of lakes — surface skimming, shoreline collection, and diver-assisted recovery — so it never reaches rivers and oceans.
Why does it matter? Lake plastic sinks out of sight, where it leaches fuel, oil, and heavy metals for decades. Recovering it protects water quality, wildlife, and the recreation millions depend on.

world.sum: Founded by ocean scientist Dr. Sylvia Earle, Mission Blue backs a community-led network of 168 Hope Spots, ocean places local champions work to protect.
eli: A Hope Spot is a special place in the ocean that needs protecting.
People who live nearby pick it and help take care of it.
There are now 168 Hope Spots in 115 countries.

world.sum: Tiny ocean plants produce about half of Earth's oxygen, making phytoplankton one of the planet's most important natural systems.
eli: What is it? A natural system that turns sunlight and carbon dioxide into food and oxygen.
Why does it matter? Healthy oceans mean breathable air and a working food web.

src.name: NOAA, How much oxygen comes from the ocean?

world.sum: Salt marshes are nurseries for more than 75% of fisheries species and buffer shorelines from erosion and floods (NOAA). Twice a day with the tides, all year.
eli: What is it? Coastal wetlands flooded and drained by the tides, with deep, spongy peat soils.
Why does it matter? They are essential for healthy fisheries, coastlines and communities.
How does it help people? Salt marshes reduce flooding by slowing and absorbing rainwater, protect shorelines from erosion, and support the seafood many communities depend on.

src.name: NOAA Ocean Service, What is a salt marsh?

world.sum: Seagrass covers just 0.1% of the seafloor but stores 11% of the ocean's buried organic carbon, and one acre can support almost 40,000 fish, NOAA says.
eli: What is it? Underwater flowering plants forming meadows.
Why does it matter? Carbon storage and fish nurseries.
world.alt: Close-up of newly planted seagrass underwater in the Banana River, Florida

world.sum: Surfrider Foundation volunteers protect the ocean, waves and beaches, and in 2025 they removed 338,383 pounds of trash from U.S. coasts (Surfrider).
eli: Surfrider is a group of people who love the beach and want it clean.
Volunteers pick up trash so it doesn't hurt sea animals.
They also count what they find to help stop plastic at the source.
world.alt: Two surfers at sunset among sea stacks and crashing waves at Second Beach in Olympic Coast National Marine Sanctuary
world.credit: Image: Matt McIntosh/NOAA (public domain)

world.sum: A worldwide science program where students and citizen scientists collect real environmental data: more than 293 million measurements from 127 countries.
eli: GLOBE lets kids and grown-ups do real science outside.
You look at clouds, trees or soil and send what you see with an app.
Scientists use your measurements to understand our planet.

world.sum: Deep-ocean buoys, satellites, GPS signals and seafloor cables spot tsunamis in the open ocean so coastal communities get time to reach high ground (NOAA, NASA).
eli: A tsunami is a group of giant waves, usually made when a big earthquake shakes the sea floor.
Buoys, satellites and special computers watch the ocean and tell warning centers when a tsunami is coming.
If the ground shakes hard or the sea pulls back fast near a beach, go to high ground right away.

src.name: NASA, SWOT satellite measures tsunami after massive quake

world.n: Three Trees for Every One Removed
world.sum: Saving Planets' own forest rule: plant three trees for every one removed, so each removal becomes a net gain for habitat, soil and shade, and is easy to verify.
eli: What is it? For every tree that comes out, three go in. That replaces what was lost and starts to rebuild habitat, soil, and shade.
Why does it matter? Removing a tree without replacement accelerates habitat loss, soil erosion, and carbon release. A three-to-one ratio turns removal into net restoration.
world.alt: Three trees for every one removed

world.sum: Whale waste carries nutrients to the ocean surface and fertilizes phytoplankton, the tiny plants at the base of the ocean food web (NOAA Fisheries).
eli: Whales eat deep in the ocean and then poop near the top.
Their poop is like plant food for tiny ocean plants.
Those plants feed fish and help take carbon out of the air.

src.name: NOAA Fisheries, Whales and carbon sequestration

world.alt: A humpback whale surfacing with gulls riding on its nose in Stellwagen Bank National Marine Sanctuary
world.credit: Image: Elliot Hazen/NOAA Fisheries Permit #14245 (public domain)
